# A
# SYSTEM
## OF
# MORAL
# PHILOSOPHY,
### IN THREE BOOKS;

->WRITTEN BY THE LATE<-
## FRANCIS HUTCHESON, LL.D. <insert>the elder</insert>
->PROFESSOR OF PHILOSOPHY<-
->IN THE UNIVERSITY OF GLASGOW.<-
->PUBLISHED FROM THE ORIGINAL MANUSCRIPT,<-
->BY HIS SON FRANCIS HUTCHESON, M.D.<-

->To which is added<-
->AN ACCOUNT OF THE LIFE, WRITINGS, AND CHARACTER OF THE AUTHOR,<-
->BY THE REVEREND WILLIAM LEECHMAN, D.D.<-
->PROFESSOR OF DIVINITY IN THE SAME UNIVERSITY.<-

## VOLUME I.

---

->**GLASGOW:** PRINTED AND SOLD BY **R.** AND **A. FOULIS** PRINTERS TO THE UNIVERSITY.<-

## LONDON,
->SOLD BY **A. MILLAR** ACROSS FROM **KATHERINE STREET** IN THE **STRAND**,<-
->AND BY **T. LONGMAN** IN **PATERNOSTER ROW**.<-
->**1755.**<-

<summary>This is the title page for the first volume of Francis Hutcheson's posthumous work on moral philosophy, which includes a biographical account of the author by William Leechman. The book was published in 1755 by the Foulis brothers in Glasgow and distributed by booksellers in London.</summary>
<keywords>Francis Hutcheson, Moral Philosophy, William Leechman, University of Glasgow, Foulis Press, 18th-century philosophy, ethics, A. Millar, T. Longman</keywords>

--- Page 3 ---
<meta>This page follows the title page of Volume I. It is a formal dedication written by the author's son, Francis Hutcheson, M.D., to Edward Synge, the Bishop of Elphin.</meta>

### TO THE RIGHT REVEREND
## FATHER IN GOD,
# EDWARD,
## LORD BISHOP OF ELPHIN.

->MY LORD,<-

**YOUR** *Lordship’s known regard for the sacred interests of Virtue and true Religion, is sufficient to ensure your favorable reception of any work which tends to promote those great and important ends. The following work has yet a further claim to your Lordship’s favor. The Author, my excellent Father (your Lordship knows I do not exceed the truth in calling him so), was formerly honored with a place in your friendship. As this was a source of the highest pleasure to him while he lived, so it must reflect particular honor upon his memory. It is with pleasure I embrace this public opportunity of declaring myself, with the highest respect and gratitude,*

->MY LORD,<-

*Your Lordship’s most obedient,*

*and most humble Servant,*

FRANCIS HUTCHESON.

DUBLIN, }
Jan. 25, 1755. }

<summary>This is a formal dedication of the book to Edward Synge, the Bishop of Elphin, written by the author's son. The son highlights the Bishop's commitment to virtue and his past friendship with the late Francis Hutcheson as reasons for the dedication.</summary>
<keywords>Edward Synge, Bishop of Elphin, Francis Hutcheson, dedication, virtue, religion, Dublin, 1755</keywords>

# CONTENTS OF THE FIRST VOLUME.

->The preface, giving some account of the life, writings, and character of the author.<-

## BOOK I.

### Concerning the constitution of human nature and the supreme good.

Chapter 1. Concerning the constitution of human nature and its powers; and first, the understanding, will, and passions. Page 1
Chapter 2. Concerning the finer powers of perception. 15
Chapter 3. Concerning the ultimate determinations of the will and benevolent affections. 38
Chapter 4. Concerning the moral sense, or faculty of perceiving moral excellence, and its supreme objects. 53
Chapter 5. The sense of honor and shame explained. The universal influence of the moral sense and that of honor; and their uniformity. 79

## BOOK I. PART II.

### An enquiry into the supreme happiness of mankind.

Chapter 6. How far the various sensations, appetites, passions, and affections are within our power. 100
Chapter 7. A comparison of the various sorts of enjoyment and the opposite sorts of uneasiness, to find their importance to happiness. 116
Chapter 8. A comparison of the various tempers and characters in terms of happiness or misery. 148

**Chapter 9.** Duties toward God; and first, of just sentiments concerning his nature. Page 168
**Chapter 10.** The affections, duty, and worship to be exercised toward the Deity. 209
**Chapter 11.** The conclusion of this book, showing the way to the supreme happiness of our nature. 221

## B O O K II.

->Containing a deduction of the more specific laws of nature,<-
->and duties of life, prior to civil government and<-
->other adventitious <note>Acquired or non-innate</note> states.<-

**Chapter 1.** The circumstances which increase or diminish the moral good or evil of actions. 227
**Chapter 2.** General rules for judging the morality of actions, based on the affections inciting them or opposing them. 238
**Chapter 3.** The general notions of rights and laws explained, along with their divisions. 252
**Chapter 4.** The different states of men. The state of liberty is not a state of war. The way that private rights are known. The necessity of a social life. 280
**Chapter 5.** The private rights of men; first, those called natural, and the natural equality of men. 293
**Chapter 6.** The adventitious <note>Rights or states that are acquired rather than innate, such as those arising from contracts</note> rights, real and personal. Property or dominion. 309
**Chapter 7.** The means of acquiring property. How far it extends. In which subjects it resides. 324
**Chapter 8.** Concerning derived property, and the ways of alienating or transferring it. 340

# THE PREFACE,

## Giving some account of the life, writings, and character of the author.

Dr. Francis Hutcheson was born on August 8, 1694. His father, Mr. John Hutcheson, was the minister of a dissenting congregation in the North of Ireland; he was a person of good understanding, considerable learning, and had a reputation for piety, probity, and every virtue. When his son Francis was about eight years of age, he was sent to be educated along with his elder brother under the supervision and direction of their grandfather, Mr. Alexander Hutcheson. Alexander was also a worthy dissenting clergyman in the same part of the country, but he had come from Scotland. He was the second son of an ancient and reputable family in the shire of Ayr in that kingdom.

A superior capacity, an ardent thirst for knowledge, and the seeds of the finest dispositions soon began to

# PREFACE.

show themselves in Francis: particularly a singular warmth of affection and disinterestedness of temper, for which he was distinguished through his whole life, appeared in many instances in this early period of it. The innocence and sweetness of his temper, his great capacity and application to his learning soon procured him a distinguished place in his grandfather’s affections. But such was his love for his brother, that his grandfather’s fondness gave him no joy while his brother did not equally share it: indeed, the preference that was shown him gave him real concern, and led him to employ all means and innocent artifices in his power to make his brother appear equally deserving of his grandfather’s regard. And when his grandfather in his last will had made an alteration of a prior settlement of his family affairs in his favor, though many arguments were used by his relations to persuade him to accept it, he peremptorily refused, and insisted to the last that the first settlement should take place. These, and many other instances of the like kind which might be related, were promising presages of remarkable disinterestedness in more advanced years.

# PREFACE.

When he had gone through the common course of school education, he was sent to an Academy at some distance from his parents to begin his course of Philosophy. He was taught there the ordinary Scholastic Philosophy which was in vogue in those days, and to which he applied himself with uncommon assiduity and diligence.

In the year 1710, he left the Academy and entered as a student in the Natural Philosophy class at the University of Glasgow; at the same time, he renewed his study of the Latin and Greek languages. In all areas of literature to which he applied himself, he made such proficiency as might be expected from a genius like his, cultivated with great care and diligence.

After he had finished the usual course of philosophical studies, his thoughts turned toward Divinity, which he intended to make the specific study and profession of his life. To pursue this goal, he continued for several more years at the University of Glasgow, studying Theology under the direction of the reverend and learned Professor John Simson.

# PREFACE.

Among the many theological inquiries that occurred to him as deserving his most serious examination, he chose to begin with the grand fundamental one concerning the being, perfections, and providence of God. The Reverend Dr. Clark’s learned and ingenious book on this subject, published a short time before, fell into his hands. Although he most heartily approved of all the Doctor’s conclusions and had the highest respect for his singular abilities and virtues, yet after the most serious and attentive consideration of his arguments, he did not find in them the conviction he wished and expected. In order to gain more satisfaction on this subject, and particularly regarding the force and solidity of the *a priori* arguments (as they are commonly called), he wrote a letter to him about the year 1717, urging his objections and desiring a further explanation. Whether the Doctor returned any answer to this letter does not appear from Dr. Hutcheson’s papers. After all the inquiry he could make, he still continued extremely doubtful of the validity and force of all the metaphysical arguments by which many have endeavored to demonstrate the existence, unity, and perfections of

He not only thought that these kinds of arguments were not suited to the capacity of the majority of mankind, but even that they could afford no solid and permanent conviction to the learned themselves. It was his opinion in this early part of his life, and he never saw cause to alter it, that as some subjects, by their nature, are capable of demonstrative evidence, so others admit only of a probable one; and that to seek demonstration where only probability can be obtained is almost as unreasonable as to demand to see sounds or hear colors. Besides, he was persuaded that attempts at demonstration on such subjects as are incapable of it were of very dangerous consequence to the interests of truth and religion: because such attempts, instead of conducting us to the absolute certainty proposed, leave the mind in such a state of doubt and uncertainty as leads to absolute skepticism: for if we once refuse to rest in that kind of evidence which the nature of the subject alone admits, and go on in pursuit of the highest kind—strict demonstration—we immediately conclude there is no evidence, because we do not find the kind of it which we expected: and thus the mind remains in a state of

It is only fair to his character to say that he was useful and contented in that position in which it had pleased Divine Providence to place him, and that neither the love of riches, nor the elegance or grandeur of human life influenced him enough to make him act against his inner convictions. To this it may be added that the silent and unseen hand of an all-wise Providence—which governs all the events of human life and all the decisions of the human will—led him to that position in life. The profession of Moral Philosophy was the department assigned to him in the College. In cultivating this science, he pursued the same method with which he began, setting aside all research into the abstract relations and eternal fitness and unfitness of things, and directing his inquiries toward what is more obvious and immediately known from observation and experience—namely, what is in fact the current constitution of human nature, and what state of heart and course of life is most consistent with its entire structure.

He had observed that it was the good fortune and glory of the present age that they had discarded the method of forming hypotheses and suppositions in natural philosophy, and had instead set themselves to make observations and experiments on the constitution of the material world itself, and to note the powers and principles which are seen operating within it. He saw plainly that it was by adhering strictly to this method that natural philosophy had been carried to a greater degree of perfection than ever before, and that

it is only by pursuing the same method that we can hope to reach higher improvements in that science. He was convinced that, in like manner, a true scheme of morals could not be the product of genius and invention, or of the greatest precision of thought in metaphysical reasonings, but must be drawn from proper observations upon the several powers and principles of which we are conscious in our own bosoms, and which must be acknowledged to operate in some degree in the whole human species. And therefore, at least one proper method to be followed in moral science is to inquire into our internal structure as a constitution or system composed of various parts, to observe the office and purpose of each part, along with the natural subordination of those parts to one another, and from there to conclude what is the design of the whole, and what is the course of action for which it appears to be intended by its great Author. He thought there was ground to hope that from a more strict philosophical inquiry into the various natural principles or natural dispositions of mankind—in the same way that we inquire into the structure of an animal body, of a plant, or of the solar system—a more

--- Page 29 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument for establishing a theory of morals based on the empirical observation of human nature's internal "frame," comparing the study of moral principles to the study of physical anatomy.</meta>

<page-num>xv</page-num>
<header>P R E F A C E .</header>

exact theory of morals may be formed than has yet appeared—and a theory, too, built upon such an obvious and firm foundation as would be satisfactory to every candid inquirer. For we can be as certain of the several parts of our internal frame from inward perception and feeling as we are of the several parts of an animal structure from ocular inspection. And we can as little doubt the ends for which at least the principal parts of our internal constitution are intended as we can doubt the ends for which the members of our body or our external senses were framed. And whatever evidence we have for the existence and perfections of the Supreme Being, we have the same evidence that the moral constitution of our nature is his work; and from this we conclude that it is most certainly his will that we should cultivate that temper of mind and pursue that course of life which most corresponds to the evident ends and purposes of his divine workmanship. And such a state of heart and plan of life that most effectively answers the end and design of all its parts must be its most perfect manner of operation and must constitute the duty, the happiness, and the perfection of the order of beings to whom it belongs.

<summary>The author argues that human moral nature is as observable and purposeful as physical anatomy, suggesting that because this constitution is the work of a Supreme Being, following its inherent design is our essential duty and the path to happiness.</summary>

--- Page 30 ---
<meta>This page outlines the specific objectives of the work, transitioning from the theoretical study of the mind's "frame" discussed on the previous page to the practical application of these principles in ethics and social laws.</meta>

<page-num>xvi</page-num>
<header>P R E F A C E.</header>

Our author has attempted in the following work, first to unfold the various principles of the human mind as they are united in a moral constitution, and from there to point out the origin of our ideas of moral good and evil, and of our sense of duty, or moral obligation. He then inquires what the supreme happiness must be for a species constituted as mankind are; and then he proceeds to deduce the particular laws of nature, or rules necessary to be observed for promoting the general good in our common interactions with one another as members of society. How far he has succeeded must be left to the judgment of the attentive and candid reader.

Whatever corrections or improvements his scheme may be supposed to admit of, after longer observation and further examination into the structure and operations of our minds, one thing is certain: that the result of his observations and reasonings must meet with entire approval, as it places the highest virtue and excellence of a human character where all sound Philosophy and Divine Revelation have placed it, namely: *In such habitual and prevailing exercise of all these good affections toward God and man as will restrain all other appetites, passions, and affections within just bounds, and*

<summary>The author outlines the work's objectives: analyzing the human mind's moral structure, defining duty and happiness, and deriving social laws to promote the general good. He argues that true virtue consists of disciplined love for God and humanity, aligning his theory with both philosophy and scripture.</summary>
<keywords>moral constitution, moral obligation, laws of nature, supreme happiness, human mind, Philosophy, Divine Revelation, virtue</keywords>

# PREFACE.

<columns>2</columns>

carry us out uniformly to *pursue* that course of action which will promote the happiness of mankind in the most extensive manner to which our power can reach*. And it must also be acknowledged that our Author's doctrine—which asserts that we are laid under a real internal obligation, of a most sacred kind, from the very constitution of our nature†, to promote the good of mankind, though at the expense of sacrificing life itself and all its enjoyments—coincides, or at least is in no way inconsistent with those precepts of Christianity by which we are enjoined to lay down our lives for the

---

<note>* Some seem to have mistaken our Author's doctrine so widely as to imagine that he placed virtue in the mere sentiment or perception of moral beauty and deformity in affections and actions, which it is admitted the worst of mankind may retain to a very considerable degree. Whereas he always places it in the exercise of these affections and the actions flowing from them which the moral faculty recommends and enjoins. Or in other words, virtue does not lie in the mere sentiment of approval of certain affections and actions, but in acting agreeably to it.</note>

<note>† Some seem to have mistaken Dr. Hutcheson so far on this subject as to imagine that when he says we are laid under a most real and intimate obligation by the moral sense to act virtuously, he meant to assert that all other obligations from the consideration of the will of God, and the effects of his favor or displeasure in this
<column-break/>
and in another world were superseded. Nothing could be further from his thoughts; nor is it a consequence of his scheme. He was fully sensible of the importance and necessity of enforcing the practice of virtue upon mankind from all possible considerations, and especially from those solemn ones of future rewards and punishments. If anyone should say that there is a natural sense of equity implanted in the human mind, which will operate to some degree even in those who do not know that there is a God or a future state: it could not justly be concluded from that that such a person also maintained that this natural sense of equity alone was sufficient to ensure the uniform practice of justice in all mankind, even when meeting with countless strong temptations to depart from it. The application is so obvious that it is unnecessary to insist upon it.</note>

According to this representation of things, the soul of man not only bears a resemblance to the Divine Intelligence in its rational faculties, but also to the Divine disinterested benignity in its social and public affections. Thus, too, our internal constitution, formed for pursuing the general good, beautifully matches the constitution of the universe. We see through the whole of Nature what admirable provision is made for carrying on the general interests of all the species of living beings. So it is quite consistent with the analogy of Nature that mankind, the highest order of creatures in this lower world, should be formed with dispositions to promote the general good of their species, and with a discernment that it is their duty to part with life itself when a public interest requires it.

He loved truth and sought after it with impartiality and constancy. His understanding was quick and his memory strong; he was not only patient in thought and inquiry, but delighted in it. His mind was never subject to that lethargy which frequently interrupts the studies of worthy men; his faculties were always at his command and ready for exercise. A mind endowed and inclined in such a manner, and employed in study over many years, must have been furnished with a wide range of knowledge.

In the earlier part of his life, he entered deeply into the spirit of the ancients, and was soon aware of and admired that precision and simplicity of both thought and expression which has preserved and distinguished their writings to this day. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; These unique abilities and talents were united in Dr. Hutcheson with the most amiable dispositions and most useful virtues: the purity of his manners was unspotted from his youth. As he always expressed the highest indignation against vice, he kept at the greatest distance from it, avoiding even the smallest indecencies of conduct. But this severity of virtue was without any of that sourness, stiffness, or unsociability which sometimes accompanies it, rendering characters who are otherwise valuable disagreeable in some respects, and preventing the good effects that the example of their virtues might produce upon others. His integrity was strict and inviolable: he abhorred the least appearance of deceit either in word or action. He despised those little artifices which too frequently pass in the world for laudable social skills and proofs of superior prudence. His nature was frank, open, and warmly disposed to speak what he took to be true: you saw at first sight his sincere and upright soul, and in all further interaction with him you found

The power of devout sentiments over his mind was evident in his conversation: in his public lectures, he frequently took the opportunity—both from hints provided by his subject and when it was the direct subject itself—to speak at great length and with great passion on the reasonableness and advantages of habitual regard for God, and of attributing all our talents, virtues, and enjoyments to his bounty. Such habitual references appeared to him to be the surest means of checking those emotions of pride, vain complacency, and self-applause which are likely to spring up in the minds of those who do not seriously and frequently reflect that they did not make themselves *to differ from others, and that they have nothing but what they received.* He looked upon such sentiments, when deeply rooted in the mind, as the proper foundation of that simplicity of heart and life which is the highest perfection of a virtuous character.

He had a great wealth of natural eloquence and a persuasive manner; he attended, indeed, much more to meaning than to expression, and yet his expression was good. He was a master of that precision and accuracy of language which is necessary in philosophical inquiries. But he did not consider it his duty, either in his lectures <note>prelections</note> or in his writings on moral and religious subjects, to strictly maintain at all times the character of the didactic teacher by confining himself to all the precision required in accurate explanation and strict argument. He believed that he was fulfilling the purpose of his office just as effectively when he spoke in a more expansive manner on such moral considerations as are suited to touch the heart and inspire a love for virtue, as when explaining or establishing any doctrine, even one of real importance, with the most philosophical exactness. He regarded the cultivation of the heart as a primary goal of all moral instruction; he kept it habitually in mind, and he was extremely well qualified for succeeding in it, as far as human means can go. It added greatly to the usefulness of his lessons that they were not confined to high speculations and the specifics of a particular system, but frequently descended to common life. He sometimes pointed out and exposed fashionable vices and follies in the upper classes, departures from real justice and equity in the busy and commercial world, and the dangerous rocks on which youth is likely to split and shipwreck both virtue and happiness; at other times, he insisted upon matters acknowledged by everyone to be of the highest importance. The grand maxims he focused on and labored to instill into the minds of his pupils were to rejoice above all things in the firm persuasion of the universal Providence of a Being infinitely wise and good, who loves all his works and cannot be conceived as hating anything he has made. He was especially eager to be helpful to the students of divinity, endeavoring, among other important instructions, to give them correct ideas of the main purpose of preaching. High speculations on disputable points, either of theology or philosophy, he looked upon as altogether improper for the pulpit, at least on all ordinary occasions. He particularly insisted upon the uselessness and impropriety of handling in the pulpit such speculative questions as whether human nature is capable of disinterested affections, whether the origin of duty or moral obligation is from natural conscience or moral sense, from law, or from rational views of interest, and similar inquiries. Such was the life of this worthy person, spent in a course of diligent but not painful study, in continually doing good to the utmost of his power, and spreading truth, virtue, and religion among mankind. To conclude, he had uncommon abilities, uncommon virtues, and small failings, and even these arose from good qualities; if he was at any time too much or too quickly provoked, it was owing to the quickness of his intellect and the sensitivity of his temper; if his indignation was strong, it was only provoked by such baseness or malice as his heart abhorred; if at any time he was open, when reserve might have been more proper, it proceeded from an honesty and sincerity of heart unaccustomed to deception. Some were displeased with his honest freedom, some might envy his reputation, some slandered him through prejudice, and some through bigotry; but his intellect, his spirit, and his worth will be remembered when any prejudices that were raised against him are entirely forgotten.

### A

## BOOK I.
### *Concerning the Constitution of* HUMAN NATURE, *and the* SUPREME GOOD.

## CHAPTER I.
### *Of the Constitution of Human Nature and its Powers, and first the Understanding, Will and Passions.*

<margin>What moral philosophy is.</margin>
I. THE INTENTION OF MORAL PHILOSOPHY IS TO direct men toward that course of action which tends most effectively to promote their greatest happiness and perfection, so far as it can be done through observations and conclusions discoverable from the constitution of nature, without any aid from supernatural revelation. These maxims or rules of conduct are therefore regarded as laws of nature, and the system or collection of them is called the LAW of NATURE.

<margin>Knowledge of human powers is necessary for it.</margin>
Since human happiness, which is the goal of this art, cannot be clearly known without a previous knowledge of the constitution of this species—and of all its perceptive and active powers and their natural objects—(as happiness signifies the state of the soul ari-

In this inquiry, we shall only briefly mention such parts of our constitution, whether in body or mind, as are not of great consequence in morals; avoiding unnecessary controversies, and often referring to other authors for those points which have been tolerably well explained by them. Thus, we pass over many clever anatomical observations upon the advantages and dignity of the human body above that of other animals. The reader may find them in the anatomical authors, and Dr. Cumberland.

Many other animals are both clothed and armed by nature, and have all that is necessary for their defense or convenient subsistence without any care or contrivance of their own: the uncultivated earth offers them their food, and the woods or rocks provide their shelter. Mankind is naked and unarmed; their more healthy and agreeable food is rarer, requiring much art and labor: their bodies are less fit to resist the damage of the weather without more laborious contrivances for clothing and shelter. Their preservation, therefore, in their tender years, must depend on the care of adults; and their lives would always continue to be miserable if they lived in solitude, without the help of their fellows.

<margin>*their final causes.*</margin>
This is no unreasonable severity in the Author of Nature toward our species. We shall soon discover the natural remedy provided for this lasting weakness of our younger years in the tender parental affection of a rational species; and the final causes <note>ultimate purposes or intended designs</note> of it in the several improvements we are capable of receiving. The means of subsistence for our species require much contrivance and ingenuity: we are capable of many noble enjoyments unknown to other animals, which depend on useful and delightful arts that we cannot attain without a long education, much instruction, and the imitation of others. How much time is required for learning our mother tongues? How much for dexterity even in the most common arts of agriculture, or in domestic service? <margin>Powers which appear first.</margin>
III. The natural principles which first reveal themselves are our external senses, along with some small powers of spontaneous motion, an appetite for food, and an instinct to receive and swallow it. All these powers operate in a way too obscure for any of us to ever fully understand; much less do animals have any knowledge to guide them to the teats of their mothers, or any concept of the air pressure upon which sucking depends. At first, indeed, we all act alike by instincts wisely implanted by a superior hand.

Our external senses soon introduce to the mind some perceptions of pleasure and pain; and along with these perceptions, there immediately appears a natural, constant determination to desire the one and repel the other; to pursue whatever appears to be the cause or occasion of pleasure, and to shun the causes of pain. These are probably our first notions of natural good or evil, of happiness or misery.

<header>EXTERNAL SENSATIONS.</header>

These sensations, as the learned agree, are not pictures or representations of similar external qualities in objects, nor of the impression or change made in the bodily organs. They are either *signals*, as it were, of new events happening to the body, of which experience and observation will show us the cause; or *marks*, established by the Author of Nature, to show us what things are beneficial, harmless, or hurtful; or intimations of things not otherwise discernible which may affect our condition; though these marks or signals bear no more resemblance to the external reality than the report of a gun, or the flash of the powder, bears to the distress of a ship. The pleasant sensations of taste, smell, and touch generally arise from objects that are harmless or beneficial when used in a moderate degree; the disagreeable or painful sensations arise from those that are harmful or unfit for common use. But sight and hearing do not seem to be immediate avenues of pain; scarcely is any visible form or any sound the immediate occasion of it; though the violent motion of light or air may cause painful feelings; and yet through sight and hearing the exquisite pleasures of beauty and harmony have access to the soul, as well as the ideas of sizes, figures, situation, and motion. It is through the former senses, and not through these, that we receive the pleasures commonly called *sensual*.

<margin>The acts of the will.</margin>
V. Although there are many other types of finer perceptions to be considered as natural to humans, yet since some of them have the acts of the *will*, the affections, and the passions as their objects, it is necessary to take a brief look at the will and its natural determinations before we proceed to these finer perceptions.

It is clear that as soon as any sense, opinion, or reasoning represents an object or event as immediately good or pleasant, or as a means of future pleasure or security from evil—either for ourselves or for any person about whom we are concerned—there arises immediately a new motion of the soul, distinct from all sensation, perception, or judgment: a *desire* for that object or event. And upon the perception or opinion of an object or event as a cause of pain or misery, or the loss of something good, there arises a contrary motion called *aversion*. On all such occasions, these primary motions of the will naturally arise without any previous choice or command, and they are the general sources of action in every rational agent.

VI. There are two calm natural determinations of the will to be particularly considered on this occasion. First, an invariable, constant impulse toward one's own perfection and happiness of the highest kind. This † instinct operates in the majority of mankind very confusedly, as they do not reflect upon, or pay attention to, their own constitution and powers of action and enjoyment; few have considered and compared the various enjoyments they are capable of, or the several powers of action. But whoever does so will find a calm, settled desire for the perfection of all our active powers, and for the highest enjoyments, such as appear to us, upon comparison, to be of the greatest importance to our happiness. Those who have not made such reflections and comparisons naturally desire all sorts of enjoyments they have any notion of through their senses or any higher powers they have exercised, as far as they are consistent with each other, or appear to be so; and they desire the perfection of such powers as they pay attention to. Where several enjoyments appear inconsistent, the mind, while it is calm, naturally pursues, or desires in preference to others, those which seem of the greatest importance to its happiness. So far all agree.

Sensations indicate only such changes, and new events or objects, as it is convenient for us to be apprised of. Thus volitions move the head, the eyes, the mouth, the tongue, the limbs, and the hand—that exquisite instrument of a rational, inventive, and artful species. All these are plain indications of the wise and benign counsel of our Creator. Indeed, our limbs are moved immediately as a consequence of the contraction of muscles and of some power sent down by nerves from the head. But in our spontaneous motions, we neither know nor will these intermediate steps: we intend the final motion, and those other motions are performed without any knowledge or will of ours. Sensation, in like manner, immediately follows some motion in a nerve continued to the brain; we perceive no motion in the brain, but have a sensation immediately referred to the extremity of the body where the impression was made, and seeming to occupy that place, in a manner quite inexplicable. These considerations have led some ingenious and pious men to conclude that a superior Being, or the Deity himself, is the sole physical cause of all our motions, according to certain general laws, and the sole efficient cause of all our sensations too, in the same manner.

## CHAPTER II.
### *Concerning the Finer Powers of Perception.*

I. After the general account of the perceptive powers and of the will, we proceed to consider some finer powers of perception, and some other natural determinations of the will, and general laws of the human constitution.

<margin>Pleasures of the imagination.</margin>
To the senses of seeing and hearing are added in most men, though in very different degrees, certain powers of perception of a finer kind than what we have reason to imagine exist in most of the lower animals, who nonetheless perceive various colors and figures and hear various sounds. These we may call the senses of beauty and harmony, or, with Mr. Addison, the *imagination*. Whatever name we give them, it is manifest that the several following qualities in objects are sources of pleasure established by nature; or, that men have natural powers or determinations to perceive pleasure from them.

<margin>Beauty.</margin>
1. Certain forms are more pleasing to the eye than others, even setting aside all pleasure from any lively colors; especially such complex forms where uniformity, or equality of proportion among the parts, is observable. Nor can we, by the command of our will, cause all forms to appear pleasant without distinction, any more than we can make all objects pleasing to the taste.

<margin>Congratulation.</margin>

We have this sympathy even with brute animals; and hence poets so successfully please us with descriptions of their joys. And all this is wisely designed, since freedom from pain seems to be a prior necessity for the enjoyment of good. <margin>A natural propensity to action in most animals,</margin>IV. Before we mention some other finer senses, which have the actions of men as their objects, we must observe one general determination of the soul to exercise all its active powers. We may see in our species, from the very cradle, a constant propensity to action and motion: children grasping, handling, viewing, and tasting everything. As they advance, they exert other powers, making all possible trials, observing all changes, and inquiring into their causes. They do this from an impulse to action and an implanted instinct toward knowledge, even when they are not allured by any prospects of advantage. Indeed, we see almost all other animals, as soon as they are born, exercising their several powers by similar instincts in the way that the Author of Nature intended; and by this exercise, though often laborious and fatiguing, they are made happier than any state of slothful sensuality could make them. Serpents try their reptile motions; beasts raise themselves and walk or run; birds attempt to raise themselves with their wings and soar on high; waterfowl take to the water as soon as they see it. <margin>chiefly in men.</margin>
Children are ever in motion while they are awake, nor do they avoid weariness and toil: they show an aversion to sleep until it overpowers them against their will. They observe whatever occurs, they remember and inquire about it; they learn the names of things, inquire into their natures, structures, uses, and causes; nor will their curiosity give way to rebukes and insults. Kind affections soon emerge toward those who are kind to them; they show strong gratitude, and an ardor to excel in anything that is praised. In competing with their peers they are overjoyed by success and victory, and exceedingly dejected when they are outdone by others. They are quickly provoked to anger by any imagined injury or hurt; they are afraid of experienced pain and provoked at the cause of it, but are soon appeased by finding it was unintentional, or by expressions of repentance. There is nothing they resent more than false accusation or reproach. They are prone to sincerity, truth, and openness of mind, until they have experienced some evils following from it. They are impatient to relate to others anything new or strange, or anything likely to cause admiration or laughter; they are ready to gratify anyone with what they have no use for themselves; they are fond of pleasing and free from suspicion, until they have had experience of injuries.

<margin>High pleasures in action.</margin>
This impulse to action continues throughout life, while we retain the use of our powers. Even men who are most worthless and slothful are not completely idle; they have their games, their private groups, and conversation.

<margin>A moral sense.</margin>
V. Action is established for mankind as the grand source of their happiness by a higher power of perception than any yet mentioned; namely, that by which they receive the moral notions of actions and characters. There was never any of the human species, except idiots, to whom all actions appeared indifferent. Moral differences in action are discerned by all, even when they consider no advantage or disadvantage resulting to themselves from them. As this moral sense is of high importance, it shall be more fully considered in a subsequent chapter. It may suffice for now to observe what we all feel: that a certain temperament, a set of affections, and the actions resulting from them, when we are conscious of them in ourselves, raise the most joyful sensations of approval and inward satisfaction; and when the same are observed in others, we have a warm feeling of approval, a sense of their excellence, and, as a consequence of it, great goodwill and zeal for their happiness. If we are conscious of contrary affections and actions, we feel an inward remorse and dislike of ourselves; when we observe the same in others, we dislike and condemn their dispositions, regarding them as base and odious.

The affections which excite this moral approval are all either directly benevolent or naturally connected with such dispositions; those which are disapproved and condemned are either ill-natured, by which one is inclined to cause misery to others; or

<margin>universal in mankind.</margin>
This moral discernment is not limited to people of fine education and much reflection. Even the most unrefined of mankind show such notions; and young minds, who think least about the distant influences of actions upon themselves or others, and have little concern for their own future interests, are actually more moved by *moral forms* than others. From this comes that strong inclination in children—as soon as they understand the names of the various affections and temperaments—to hear stories that present the moral characters of individuals and their fates. From this comes that joy in the prosperity of the kind, the faithful, and the just; and that indignation and sorrow upon the successes of the cruel and treacherous. We shall treat this power more fully later.

<margin>A sense of honour;</margin>
VI. Just as we are led by the former determination to approve or condemn ourselves or others according to the temperament displayed, so by another natural determination—which we may call a sense of honor and shame—a high pleasure is felt when we gain the approval and esteem of others for our good actions, and when they express their sentiments of gratitude. On the other hand, we are cut to the heart by censure, condemnation, and reproach. All of this appears in the facial expression. The fear of infamy, censure, or contempt reveals itself through blushing.

<page-num>26</page-num>
# SENSE of HONOR.

### BOOK I.

<margin>an immediate principle.</margin>
It is true, we may observe from our infancy that men are prone to do good deeds for those they approve of and honor. But we appeal to the hearts of men, whether they do not have an immediate pleasure in being honored and esteemed, without thinking of any future advantages, and even when they already know that they can receive none. Are we not generally concerned about our reputations after our death? And why is it that blushing accompanies this sort of fear, and not the fears of other disadvantages, if this is not an immediate principle?

* ARISTOTLE'S account of this pleasure, though more elegant, is not accurate:

> "that we relish honor as it is a testimony to our virtue, which we are already conscious is the greatest good."

This consideration may sometimes make honor very pleasing to men who are doubtful and unsure of their own conduct. But do not also the men of greatest abilities, who are perfectly assured of the goodness of their conduct, have a similar natural joy in being praised, distinct from their inward self-approval?

The kind intention of God in implanting this principle is obvious. It is a strong incentive to everything excellent and amiable: it gives a pleasing reward to virtue: it often overcomes the obstacles to it from low worldly interests: and even men of little virtue are moved by it to such useful services as they would have otherwise declined. The selfish are thus, beyond their inclination, made subservient to a public interest; and those who counteract it are punished.

<margin>The happiness of active beings is in action.</margin>
Thus, according to the just observation of <term>ARISTOTLE</term>, "The chief happiness of active beings must arise from action; and that not from action of every sort, but from that sort to which their nature is adapted, and which is recommended by nature."

When we gratify the bodily appetites, there is an immediate sense of pleasure, such as the animals enjoy, but no further satisfaction; no sense of dignity upon reflection, and no high regard for others for their being thus employed. There is an exercise of some other bodily powers which seems more manly and graceful. There is a manifest gradation; some fine tastes in the ingenious arts are still more agreeable; the exercise is delightful; the works are pleasant to the spectator and reputable for the artist. The exercise of the higher powers of the understanding, in the discovery of truth and just reasoning, is more estimable when the subjects are important. But the noblest of all are the virtuous affections and actions, the objects of the moral sense.

<page-num>30</page-num>
<header>ASSOCIATIONS *of* IDEAS.</header>

### **Book I.**
---

Inanimate objects have obtained additional ideas of dignity, decency, and sanctity; some appear as mean and despicable, and others are in a middle state of indifference. Our relish for imitation and for observing resemblances has made all languages full of metaphors; and similitudes and allegories give no small pleasure in many compositions. Hence, we clothe many objects with additional ideas of qualities they are not naturally capable of; some of these ideas are great and venerable, others low and contemptible. Some attempt to explain the natural cause or occasion of laughter—a commotion of mind that is generally agreeable, of which all are susceptible—as arising from a natural sense of the *ridiculous* in objects or events.

<margin>*Association of ideas is very necessary.*</margin>

VIII. Before we pass to the dispositions of the will, we may observe a natural, involuntary determination to associate or bind together all such perceptions as have often occurred together, or have made a strong impression on the mind at once, so that they shall still accompany each other whenever any object afterwards excites any one or more of them. As this is experienced in smaller matters, it also affects our apprehensions of natural and moral good and evil. When the tone of conversation and popular maxims have long represented certain actions or events as good, and others as evil, we find it difficult to break the association, even after our reason is convinced of the contrary. Thus, certain actions are confusedly imagined to be honorable and others dishonorable; certain stations are thought miserable and others happy; just as ghosts are imagined to be in churchyards.

<header>The WILL and HABITS.</header>

<margin>Chap. I. <image-desc>A decorative wavy line flourish.</image-desc></margin>
Although many miseries and vices spring from this source, we may see the absolute necessity of this determination. Without it, we could have little use for memory, recollection, or even speech. How tedious it would be to need a specific recollection for every word we hear or wish to speak, just to find what words and ideas are joined by the custom of the language? It would be as tedious a task as deciphering a code after we had found an alphabet. Instead, now, the sound and the idea are so associated that the one is always accompanied by the other. Indeed, how is it that we remember? When we are questioned about a past event, the time, or place, some circumstance, or a person present then, is suggested in the question, and these bring with them the whole train of associated ideas. When the subject of a debate is suggested, a man familiar with it finds, almost before any act of volition, the principal arguments on both sides arising in his mind. The power of education is largely due to this disposition, as it forms many associations in our early years; and few have the patience or courage to examine whether they are founded in nature or in the weakness of our instructors.

of our nature, by which the frequent repetition of actions gives not only a facility in performing them, by increasing our active powers, but makes the mind more prone to them for the future, or more uneasy when it is by force restrained from them. And this is called a habit. In our passive sensations, pleasures and pains are rather abated by frequent feelings; and yet the uneasiness resulting from the lack of pleasures is increased by our being long inured to them. If we find much detriment from habits of vice, equally great is the advantage of the habits of virtue. It is of general advantage to a rational species that it can thus increase any of its powers as it chooses, and make them more stable and vigorous. It is still in our power, too, to wear out any habits by abstaining from their acts, or by resolutely acting in opposition to them. Could we acquire no habits, our powers would remain miserably weak, and all artificial action would continue to be as uneasy as we found our first attempts.

<margin>No habit or custom gives new ideas.</margin>
But all these associations, habits, customs, or prejudices recommend objects to our liking, or raise aversions to them, under the notion of some quality or type perceivable by the senses we are naturally endowed with; nor can they raise any new ideas. No sentiments, therefore, of approbation or condemnation, no liking or disliking, are sufficiently explained by attributing them to prejudice, custom, education, or association of ideas, unless we can fully show what these ideas or notions are, and to what sense they be—

<margin>
CHAPTER 2.
---
Conjugal and parental affections.
</margin>

X. At a certain age, a new desire arises between the sexes, clearly intended for the continuation of our race. Because it would be harmful or useless in our first years—before we have acquired sufficient knowledge and experience to care for offspring—it is wisely postponed in the natural order. In humans, this desire does not end merely with sensual pleasure, as it does in animals; nor is it in humans only a blind impulse, like that which excites animals before they have experienced pleasure. There is a natural liking of beauty as an indication of temperament and manners. A character is perceived, and from that, goodwill and esteem arise, along with a desire for lifelong companionship, friendship, mutual love, and shared interests. Toward offspring, there is in humans, as in other animals, a uniquely strong affection and a tender concern for their preservation and happiness. In humans, this affection continues throughout life, as parents can always do some good for their descendants. It descends to grandchildren and their children almost undiminished. Among animals, it is found where the young need assistance; where they do not, it is not found. It lasts until the young can support themselves and then generally ceases. <margin>Men are social, and fit for civil society.</margin>

One can scarcely deny that mankind has a natural impulse toward society with their fellows as an immediate principle, since we see the same in many species of animals; nor should we attribute all association to their need. Their other principles—their curiosity, communicativeness, desire for action; their sense of honor, their compassion, benevolence, gaiety, and the moral faculty—could have little or no exercise in solitude, and therefore might lead them to associate together, even without an immediate or ultimate impulse, or a sense of their own need. The ties of blood would have the same effect, and probably first united large numbers for mutual assistance and defense, upon a common fear of the hardships of solitude. When many were thus associated, the superior goodness, prudence, or courage of some would naturally earn them superior esteem and confidence from all those around them. <margin>The causes of vice.</margin>
XIII. Even though all these nobler powers we mentioned are natural to us, the causes of the vice and depravity of conduct we observe are quite obvious. Without mentioning causes that cannot be discovered by the light of nature, humanity spends many of its first years—where there is not a careful education—satisfying its sensual appetites and exercising some lower powers which, through long indulgence, grow stronger. Reflecting on moral concepts and the more refined enjoyments, and comparing them with lower pleasures, is a difficult task. Appetites and passions arise on their own whenever their objects appear, which happens frequently; restraining, examining, and balancing them is a difficult work. Prejudices and baseless associations of ideas occur very frequently to people who pay little attention. Our selfish passions quickly gain strength through indulgence. Therefore, the general course of human life is an inconsistent mixture of many social, kind, and innocent actions, and of many selfish, angry, and sensual ones, as one or another of our natural dispositions happens to be triggered and becomes dominant over others.

## *Concerning the Ultimate Determinations of the Will, and Benevolent Affections.*

<margin>The ultimate determinations of the soul.</margin>
I. After this long list of the various senses or powers of perception, by which a great multitude of objects may cause pleasure or pain, or some sorts of happiness or misery; and a similar list of many dispositions of the will, or determinations of desire; human nature must appear to be a very complex and confusing structure, unless we can discover some order and hierarchy among these powers, and thus discern which of them is naturally fit to govern. We shall treat this in the following chapters. In the first place, the *Understanding*—or the power of reflecting, comparing, and judging—makes us capable of discerning the tendencies of the various senses, appetites, actions, and gratifications, either toward our own happiness or toward that of others, as well as the relative values of every object and every gratification. This power judges the means or the secondary goals; but concerning the ultimate ends, there is no reasoning. We pursue them by some immediate disposition or determination of the soul, which in the order of action is always prior to all reasoning; for no opinion or judgment can move us to action where there is no prior desire for some end.

<margin>The selfish general determination alleged as the only one.</margin>

<margin>Various accounts of it.</margin>
This is a favorite tenet of a great many authors, and pleases by its simplicity. But very different and contrary accounts are given by these authors of the private enjoyments or happiness pursued in the offices we commonly repute virtuous. Some make the sole motive to all offices or actions, even the most honorable, the sole end ultimately intended by them, to be some worldly advantage, some bodily pleasures, or the means of achieving them. This was the tenet of the *Cyrenaicks*, and probably of the *Epicureans* too, and of some moderns. Others say that we desire the good of others, or of societies, merely as the means of our own safety and prosperity; others, as the means of some subtler pleasures of our own by sympathy with others in their happiness: others make our end to be the pleasures we enjoy in being honored, or some rewards we expect for our services, and these either from GOD, or men.

<margin>In desires, the uneasiness differs from the motives.</margin>
II. *Calm self-love*, or the determination of each individual toward his own happiness, is a movement of the *will* without any uneasy sensation attending it. But the various selfish desires, terminating on particular objects, are generally attended by some uneasy, turbulent sensations in very different degrees; yet these sensations are different from the act of the will to which they are joined, and different too from the motives of desire. The motive is some good perceived in an object or event, toward which good the desire tends; and, as a consequence of desire, some uneasiness arises until the good is obtained. In aversion, the *motive* is some evil perceived or feared, and perhaps not yet felt. Uneasiness also attends the aversion until the evil is repelled. Prospects of the pleasures or powers attending opulence are the motives for the desire of wealth, and never the uneasy feelings attending the desire itself. These feelings are, in nature, subsequent to the desire.

Men who have been careless about virtue and piety are often observed, upon the approach of danger and on other occasions, to wish heartily—out of self-love or fear of punishment—that they had love and gratitude toward God, warm charity and goodwill toward their neighbors, a meek and forgiving temperament, and sorrow for their sins; and yet they have a distressing consciousness that these dispositions do not arise in them. <margin>All kind affections do not come from sympathy.</margin>

<margin>Compassion is not selfish.</margin>
It is plain that our compassion toward the distressed also ends in their relief, even when we are not paying attention to our own pain. Nor does any desire end merely with the removal of the uneasiness that accompanies it. Thus, although there may be some natural connections of interest between us and the objects of our tender affections, the affection still ends in their good; it exists before this connection and is the cause of it. We therefore rejoice in the happiness of our child, our friend, or our country because we previously felt an ultimate goodwill toward them. We do not love them or wish them well simply because we have observed that we would derive joy from their happiness and sorrow from their misery. Consequently, the stronger our previous love and esteem were, the greater our joy will be on account of their happiness, and our sorrow for their misery.

<margin>Some affections are entirely disinterested.</margin>
This may be enough to establish the important point that our nature is capable of truly disinterested affections in the strictest sense, which are not directly subordinate to self-love or aimed at any kind of private interest. Family ties, benefits received, and moral excellence displayed are the natural causes of these particular kind affections, even though we perceive no advantage coming to ourselves from them. Many of these arise without being earned; all end in the good of others; and all of them often operate in the soul when it has no

<margin>Calm affections and passions.</margin>
VI. As we observed previously, the particular motions of the will toward one's private good are either calm, stable affections or turbulent passions. The particular motions of a generous nature are similar: some of them are calm, sedate, and steady, aiming at the happiness of their object—whether an individual or a society—and are accompanied by no turbulent sensations, only causing uneasiness when they are defeated in their intention. Others are turbulent and accompanied by uneasy sensations. We may proceed further with this comparison.

<margin>Universal benevolence.</margin>
Just as there is found in the human mind, when it reflects upon itself, a calm general determination toward the highest kind of personal happiness of which it has any concept, we may also find a similar principle of a generous kind. When, upon reflection, we present to our minds the concept of the greatest possible system of sensitive beings and the highest happiness it can enjoy, there is also a calm determination to desire it, regardless of any connection to or subservience to our own private enjoyment. We shall find these two great determinations—one toward our own greatest happiness and the other toward the greatest general good—to be independent of each other. Each is capable of enough strength to restrain all the particular affections of its kind and keep them subordinate to itself.

# CHAP. IV.

## *Concerning the Moral Sense, or the faculty of perceiving moral excellence and its supreme objects.*

<margin>The concept of moral goodness is not that it gives us pleasure through sympathy;</margin>
I. Although we have kind affections ultimately aiming at the good of others, the success of which is joyful to us, yet our approval of moral conduct is very different from liking it merely as the occasion of pleasure to ourselves in satisfying these kind affections. Just as we do not approve of all conduct which gives us this pleasure, we sometimes approve of such conduct as does not give it; and our approval of the good conduct which gives this pleasure is not proportional to the pleasure it gives us. Thus, many inventions and much art and industry which benefit the persons or country we love are not approved as virtuous: we approve of generous attempts though unsuccessful; we approve of the virtues of enemies, which may hurt the primary objects of our love. We equally approve of the virtues or generous designs of good men in former ages toward their contemporaries, or in the most remote nations toward their countrymen—for whom our affections are very faint and weak—as if the same were done for our friends or country, the objects of our strongest affections.

<margin>Not conformity to laws;</margin>
III. The primary notion under which we approve is not merely a *conformity to the divine will or laws*. We seriously inquire about the moral goodness, justice, holiness, and rectitude of the Divine Nature itself, and likewise of His will or laws; these characteristics make up our common praises of them. They surely mean more than that *His will or laws are conformable to themselves*. This we might ascribe to an artful, impure demon. Conformity to His nature is not conformity to immensity, eternity, or omnipotence. It is conformity to His goodness, holiness, and justice. These moral perfections, then, must be previously known, or else the definition by *conformity to them* is useless.

<margin>nor conformity to truth.</margin>
Neither is the notion of moral goodness under which we approve it well explained by the conformity of affections and actions to *truth, reason, true propositions, or the reason of things*; as in common acceptance, these characteristics apply to every object of the mind about which it judges truly, whether animate or inanimate, virtuous or vicious. *Conformity to moral truth*, or true propositions about morals, equally belongs to virtue and vice, as the mind discerns truth about both; and, just as every true proposition is conformed to its object, so is the object conformed to the proposition. The moral sense is destined to govern our other powers.

VI. This moral sense, by its very nature, appears to be designed for regulating and controlling all our powers. We are immediately conscious of this dignity and commanding nature, just as we are conscious of the power itself. Nor can such matters of immediate feeling be proved in any other way than by appeals to our hearts. <note>Thus the *Stoic* in *Cicero's De Finibus*, Book 3, Chapter 10: "This good of which we treat is indeed to be valued most highly, but that valuation is based on its kind, not its magnitude. ... The valuation of virtue is of a different kind, which is valid by its nature, not by its degree."</note> It does not estimate the good it recommends as merely differing in degree—though of the same kind—from other advantages recommended by other senses, so as to allow us to practice smaller moral evils (admitting them to remain such) in order to obtain some great advantages of other types; or to omit what we judge in the present case to be our duty or morally good so that we may avoid great evils of another kind. But just as we immediately perceive the difference in kind—and that the dignity of enjoyment from fine poetry, painting, or from knowledge is superior to the pleasures of the palate, no matter how delicate they might be—so we immediately discern moral good to be superior in kind and dignity to all others which are perceived by the other perceptive powers.

### Book I.

...inferior enjoyments to the superior ones; and our sense of the superior, after the first flutter of joy in our success is over, is not a bit increased by any sacrifice we have made to it. Indeed, in the judgment of spectators, the superior enjoyment—or at least our condition—is generally considered worse on this account, and our conduct is less appreciated. Thus, in sacrificing ease, health, or pleasure for wealth, power, or even the ingenious arts, those pleasures gain no dignity by that means, and the conduct is not more attractive to others. But in moral good, the greater the necessary sacrifice made for it, the more the moral excellence increases; it is more approved by the agent, more admired by spectators, and they are more inspired to imitation. By this sense, the heart can not only approve of itself in sacrificing every other gratification for moral goodness, but can also have the highest self-enjoyment and approval of its own disposition in doing so. This plainly shows that this moral sense is naturally destined to command all the other powers.

<margin>A propriety and a dignity distinct from virtue.</margin>
VIII. There is a clear progression in the objects of our approval and condemnation, from the range of indifferent actions ascending to the highest virtue, or descending to the lowest vice. It is not easy to determine exactly the various intermediate steps in their proper order, but the highest and lowest are obvious. The indifferent dispositions and actions are those that pursue the innocent advantages of the agent without any harm to society, and yet without any reference made by the agent to the good of others. These include the necessary and moderate satisfactions of appetite, and many trivial actions. To explain the different degrees, we must observe—as was hinted at previously—that besides the moral approval of virtue, there is also another appreciation or sense of a certain dignity or propriety in many dispositions and actions not conceived as virtuous. Thus we value the pursuit of the creative arts and of knowledge—indeed even some bodily perfections, such as strength and agility—more than mere animal sensuality. In the same way, we value more in another person activity, endurance of labor, wisdom, and energy in business—provided they are not harmful—even though we believe they are exercised solely for his own advancement to wealth and honor, than we value a lazy, inactive idleness.

*Qualities neither approved as virtue, nor condemned as vice.*
</margin>

The calm desire for private good, though it is not approved as virtue, is yet far from being condemned as vice. And none of the truly natural and selfish appetites and passions are in themselves condemned as evil when they are within certain bounds, even though they are not directed by the person toward any public interest. It was necessary for the general good that all such affections should be implanted in our species; therefore, it would have been utterly unnatural to have made them a matter of disapproval while they were not harmful. Indeed, as these selfish affections aim at an end necessary to the general good—namely, the good of each individual—and as the ability to satisfy them constitutes powers which may be very usefully employed in service to the most generous affections, it was highly proper and kind in the Author of Nature to invite us to cultivate these powers by an immediate taste for them wherever we observe them, in ourselves or in others; though this taste is clearly different from moral approval.

We all have, through consciousness and experience, a notion of the human constitution and of a certain proportion of affections required for an innocent character. Selfish affections are only disapproved of when we imagine them to be beyond that innocent proportion, such that they exclude or overpower the kind affections and consume the mind entirely for selfish purposes, or even obstruct the proper degree of generous affections expected in the position and circumstances of the person.

<summary>This page explains that natural selfish desires are not inherently vicious, as they are necessary for individual survival and the general good of species. These self-interested passions only become morally offensive when they exceed a natural balance and begin to suppress a person's benevolent impulses.</summary>

<margin>Degrees of virtue; first, some abilities and dispositions distinct from kind affections.</margin>
**Book I.** IX. But there is another set of dispositions and abilities of an even finer nature, though distinct from both calm universal benevolence and particular kind affections. These, however, are naturally connected with such affections, serve as natural evidence of them, and are plainly inconsistent with the highest sorts of selfishness and sensuality. These seem to be immediate objects of the *moral sense*, though perhaps not the highest ones. They seem to be approved immediately, even before we think of this connection with disinterested affections or imagine directly that the agent is directing them toward beneficent purposes. Of these moral dispositions, there are several kinds, all immediately approved unless the mind directly perceives that they are being employed for vicious purposes. Thus, fortitude is approved, as it implies that something moral is valued more than life, and it is clearly inconsistent with extreme selfishness. If, indeed, it is seen being used for robbery and merely selfish purposes, such as those of lust or greed, it becomes an object of horror. Candor, openness of mind, and sincerity can scarcely ever exist without a kind and honest heart, as it is virtue and innocence alone that require no disguise. And these dispositions are also immediately approved, perhaps before we even consider this connection; the same is true for a steadfast principle of veracity whenever we speak.

<header>APPROBATION *and* CONDEMNATION.</header>

Extensive affections are more approved than narrow ones.
</margin>
among affections that are similar in this respect, we approve more of those which are more extensive, and approve less of those which are more confined. Thus, a stable conjugal and parental love—or the resolute, calm purpose of promoting the true happiness of those related to us—is preferable to turbulent, passionate dispositions of tenderness. And the love of a society or a country is more excellent than domestic affections. We clearly see the superior dignity in these cases because, despite the struggle felt in our hearts and the opposition made by passionate or more limited affections, when we resolutely follow the calm and extensive principle despite this opposition, the soul in its calmest hours and most deliberate reflections approves of its own conduct. It scarcely ever fails to immediately approve of similar conduct in others, since, in the case of others, our own passions are not stirred to offer opposition. On the contrary, when we have yielded to passion or limited affection in opposition to a calm or more extensive principle, the soul, upon reflection, is dissatisfied with itself and, at first glance, condemns similar conduct in others.

<margin>The chief moral excellence: universal goodwill,</margin>
The disposition, therefore, which is most excellent and naturally gains the highest moral approval is a calm, stable, universal goodwill toward all, or the most extensive benevolence. And this seems to be the clearest concept we can form of the moral excellence of the Deity.

Here the agent may have no ill-will; indeed, he may have many generous affections, though not of that heroic strength which the moral sense would recommend. The guilt is greatly mitigated by the intensity of the temptation, which few have sufficient strength of soul to resist. In order to retain the character of innocence, we expect not only the absence of all malicious dispositions, but many good affections—and those, too, of an extensive nature—along with much caution concerning the interests of others. The precise degrees cannot easily be determined, nor is it necessary. But the stronger and more extensive the generous affections are, the better the character; the weaker they are, and the more that any opposite or narrower ones prevail against them, the worse the character is.

<page-num>74</page-num>
<header>ORDER among our AFFECTIONS.</header>

BOOK I.
Our moral faculty must be strangely asleep where the desire to know the Supreme Excellence is lacking, or love for it when it is known; or where there is no care to cultivate devout affections of gratitude when the greatest benefits have been received, and when they are repeated every moment.

There is a disposition still worse, conceivable in the abstract but scarcely occurring in mankind or the creatures of a good Deity: a fixed, unprovoked, original malice, or a desire for the misery of others for its own sake, without any motives of self-interest.

<margin>The moral sense brings all our powers into order.</margin>
XII. Without a clear consideration of this moral faculty, a species endowed with such a variety of senses and of frequently conflicting desires must appear to be a complex, confused structure, lacking any order or regular, consistent design. By means of it, everything is capable of harmony, and all its powers may work together in one direction and be consistent with each other. It has already been proved that we are capable of many generous affections ultimately aiming at the good of others, neither arising from any selfish view nor ending in private good. This moral faculty plainly shows that we are also capable of a calm, settled, universal benevolence, and that this is destined, as the supreme determination of our generous nature, to govern and control our specific generous affections as well as our selfish ones; just as the heart must entirely approve of it doing so in its calmest reflections. <margin>Calm self-love not the supreme principle.</margin>
To acknowledge the several generous ultimate affections of a limited kind to be natural, and yet maintain that we have no general controlling principle but self-love—which indulges or checks the generous affections as they lead to, or oppose, our own noblest interest; sometimes allowing these kind affections their full exercise, because of that high enjoyment we expect for ourselves in gratifying them; at other times checking them, when their gratification does not overbalance the loss we may sustain by it—is a scheme which brings indeed all the powers of the mind into one direction by means of the reference made of them all to the calm desire of our own happiness, in our previous deliberations about our conduct: and it may be justly alleged that the Author of Nature has made a connection in the event at last between our gratifying our generous affections, and our own highest interest. But the feelings of our heart, reason, and history, revolt against this account: which seems however to have been maintained by excellent authors and strenuous defenders of the cause of virtue.

This connection of our own highest interests with the gratifying our generous affections, in many cases is imperceptible to the mind; and the kind heart acts from its generous impulse, not thinking of its own interest. Nay, all its own interests have sometimes appeared to it as opposite to, and inconsistent with the generous part, in which it persisted. Now were there

If it is said “that it is a mistake to imagine our interest is opposite to them while there is a good providence,” grant it to be a mistake; this is only a defect of reasoning. This is plainly contrary to the feelings of our hearts.

<margin>Another ultimate determination of the will toward the public good.</margin>
Can that be deemed the sole ultimate determination, the sole ultimate end, which the mind—in the exercise of its noblest powers—can calmly resolve to deliberately counteract with inward approbation? Are there not instances of men who have voluntarily sacrificed their lives for the sake of their friends or their country, without thinking of any other state of existence? Does not every heart approve this temperament and conduct, and admire it all the more when there is less suspicion that the love of glory, posthumous fame, or any more sublime private interest is mixing itself with the generous affection? Does not the admiration rise higher the more deliberately such resolutions are formed and executed? In those cases where some inconsistency appears between these two determinations, the moral faculty at once points out and recommends the glorious, amiable part; not by suggesting prospects of future interests of a sublime sort through pleasures of self-approbation or of praise. It recommends the generous part by an immediate, undefinable perception; it approves the kind ardor of the heart in sacrificing even life itself, and that even in those who have no hopes of surviving, or no attention to a future life in another world. And thus, where the moral sense is in its full vigor, it makes the generous determination toward public happiness the supreme one in the soul, with that commanding power which it is naturally destined to exercise.

It must be obvious we are not speaking here of the ordinary condition of mankind, as if these calm determinations were generally exercised and habitually controlled the particular passions; but of the condition our nature can be raised to by due culture, and of the principles which may and ought to operate when, by attention, we present to our minds the objects or representations fit to excite them. Some good men have practiced in life only specific kind affections and found a constant approval of them, without having either the most extensive views of the whole system or the most universal benevolence.
