### C H A P. V.

#### *The Sense of Honor and Shame explained. The universal influence of the Moral Sense, and that of Honor, and their uniformity.*

<margin>Sense of honor an immediate principle.</margin>
I. If we consult our own feelings, we must acknowledge that just as there are certain affections and actions which we naturally approve, esteem, and praise, so there is an immediate pleasant sensation felt when we are approved and praised by others, and generally a most uneasy one when we are censured; without the expectation of any other advantages or disadvantages which may result from it. A more distinct consideration of this sense of honor and shame will much confirm the preceding account of our *moral faculty*.

<margin>Abstracted from private interest.</margin>
Those who refer all the motions of the heart to private interest, and would reduce all our perceptive powers to a very small number by one artful reference or another, depart exceedingly from nature in their accounts of those determinations about honor and shame, which are acknowledged to appear universally among men.

> "They tell us 'our honoring a man is merely judging him useful to us either explicitly, and thus we honor the generous and beneficent with whom we have intercourse and by whose services we are profited; or implicitly, and by some confused imaginations, and thus we honor *heroes* who lived in prior ages, or remote nations, imagining they are our contemporaries or countrymen; or thinking that they would be very useful to us if we had intercourse with them. Is all the overwhelming sense of shame, and blushing, only a fear of some future uncertain losses, which we do not know well what they shall be, or how they will befall us? <margin>This sense appears very early.</margin>
II. There is, therefore, an immediate sense of honor and shame, often operating where there are no such views of interest, and plainly presupposing a *moral sense*. It generally appears very early in life, before any considerable reasoning or reflection can properly settle the notions of morality; and thus before we can judge for ourselves, we are wisely and kindly subjected to the direction of others, are rewarded for our compliance by a most grateful sensation, and by a most uneasy one deterred from perverseness and obstinacy. The selfish explanations of this principle make all the ardor for glory the same base temperament as that of a traitor or informer, who desires to appear useful to others in hopes of a reward. They can give no better notion of modesty, the sense of shame, and the abhorrence of any imputation of moral turpitude—that *pudor* of the ROMANS, the finest stroke in a character.

<margin>*There are several degrees of the honorable and shameful.*</margin>
We see that this sense of *honor* admits several degrees in conformity with the *moral sense* on which it is founded. But first, as a consequence of that natural desire or impulse toward the perfection of all our powers, and a sense of dignity and decency in some of them above others, we find a natural pleasure in revealing to others the perfection of any manly powers and in being valued in that respect. Hence, a taste for the ingenious arts of music, sculpture, painting, and even for manly recreations, is reputable. The grandeur and elegance of living—in dress, architecture, furniture, and gardens—are, in certain circumstances, matters of glory and of praise; even more so are higher abilities, such as a strong genius for acquiring knowledge or the vivid, high imagination of the poet or orator. This last, indeed, plainly includes a high moral sense.

But to come directly to our sense of pleasure in obtaining moral approval: all actions that proceed from any friendly or kind affection, and are not opposed to some more extensive affection, are attended with confidence and openness of behavior, and we glory in them. Sensual passions and ill-natured emotions like anger, malice, envy, and even cold selfishness, we naturally conceal and are ashamed of.

<margin>*The modesty of the sexes is natural.*</margin>

As they would approve of all humanity and kindness, even when practiced toward others, and abhor the opposite dispositions, they would soon despise sensuality and selfishness. As soon as they knew how the human race is preserved, they would desire marriage and offspring; and when the occasion of this natural modesty was felt, and the intention of the appetite known, this natural check of shame would reveal itself.

How this sense is affected by education.

IV. Having a natural capacity for moral notions, we may be ashamed of actions without knowing the true reasons why they are immoral. Through education, we may acquire groundless prejudices or opinions about the qualities perceivable by any of our senses, as if they were inherent in objects where they are not. <margin>The moral sense and that of honor affect all parts of life.</margin>
V. The force of the *moral sense*, and that of *honor*, is diffused through all parts of life. The very luxury of the table derives its main charms from some mixture of moral enjoyments—from communicating pleasures, and notions of something honorable as well as elegant. How universally despicable is the character of one who, in solitude, eagerly pursues the pleasures of the palate without society or hospitality.

The chief pleasures of history and poetry, and the powers of eloquence, are derived from the same sources. History, as it represents the moral characters and fortunes of great individuals and of nations, is always exercising our *moral faculty* and our social feelings regarding the fortunes of others. Poetry entertains us in a way that is even more affecting, by providing more striking representations of the same objects in fictitious characters, and by moving our terror, compassion, and moral admiration. The power of the orator consists in moving our approval or condemnation, and the ensuing feelings of esteem or indignation, by fully presenting all the moral qualities of actions and characters. He presents all the pitiable circumstances which may extenuate or excuse a situation to engage our favor, or all the aggravating ones to increase our indignation; he displays all the vivid colors on both sides, whether he is offering praise or making invectives.

The chief beauties of countenance, and even of behavior, arise * from indications of some sweet affections, or morally estimable abilities, as is apparent by almost all the terms of praise. But we find that beauty first raises some favorable notions of an inward temperament; and, if acquaintance confirms them, we feel a high esteem and a desire for mutual friendship. In a similar way, it is some perceived *moral worth*, some justice or goodness of intention in people and causes, that occasions most of that keen zeal for certain parties and factions, and those strong attachments to them, among people who have no hope for the advantages that the leaders of those parties may have in view.

<margin>Our intimacies do not arise from self-interest.</margin>
To claim that our * choosing knowledgeable, courteous, and good-natured people for our intimates, and our avoiding the ignorant, the morose, or the selfish, proves that all our intimacies arise from selfish views, is plainly unjust. It is true that the first sort of companions are improving, pleasant, obliging, and safe; while the others are useless, unpleasant, or dangerous. But are all friendships and intimacies merely a facade and hypocrisy? Does one feel no inward esteem for certain characters and goodwill toward the people themselves? Does one only desire his own improvement, pleasure, or gain—as when he hires a teacher to instruct him in a mechanical art, or a musician to entertain him, or a laborer to perform a piece of common work? Do we only intend to maintain a fair outward appearance with our best friends so that we may not lose these advantages? On the contrary, does not everyone feel an inward esteem and goodwill toward any virtuous acquaintances, which remains even when we are separated and have no hope of meeting them again?

<margin>Intangible things are the most real.</margin>
It is worth our notice here that, although through the early prejudices of our external senses we are prone to imagine little reality in anything that is not the object of one or another of them, and to conceive what is not thus perceptible to be fictitious and imaginary; yet if we attend to the inward feelings of our hearts, the greatest realities—our very happiness and misery, that dignity or worth in which alone we can have the most complete satisfaction with ourselves, or for which we love, esteem, and admire another, and consider him excellent or happy, or choose him as a friend—are qualities entirely imperceptible. They are too noble and excellent to fall under the awareness of those powers which are primarily intended for the support of the body.

<margin>These senses are uniform.</margin>
VI. Many suspect that no such senses can be natural because there are such different and opposite notions of morality among different nations. But even granting that their tastes were different, and that different men and nations approved and condemned actions for different reasons or under different concepts, this only proves that their senses are not uniform, and not that no such principles are natural. In approving or justifying actions, in all nations, men generally claim some tendency toward the happiness of others, some kind intention of greater or lesser extent, some generous affections, or some dispositions naturally connected with them. When we excuse any imprudent conduct, we say the agent intended well; did not foresee the bad consequence; or had such provocation as might have overwhelmed even a kind disposition, or a man of justice. When we speak out against bad conduct, we show that all the opposite affections or dispositions were demonstrated by it, such as cruelty, anger, excessive selfishness, or a lack of the kind affections that we generally expect in our species. If we blame imprudent conduct without this reference to evil affections, or to the lack of good ones, it is sometimes out of our goodwill and pity toward the agent, combined with some contempt for his meager abilities, his laziness, stupidity, or indolence. And yet, how are we softened by the thought that "the poor creature intended no harm, or caused none to others." This is often indeed a false excuse, as the public suffers by anyone making himself less capable of serving it, as well as his more personal friends.

<margin>The causes of different approvals and censures; different notions of happiness.</margin>
VII. The chief causes of different approvals are these three:
1. Different notions of happiness and the means of promoting it. Nations unfamiliar with the improvements that life receives from art and industry may see no reason for encouraging them by securing to each man a right to property in the fruits of his labors, as long as the bare necessities of life are easily obtained. Indeed, they can see no harm in depriving men of their artificial acquisitions and stores beyond their current use, or of luxuries tending to dissolve them into pleasure and laziness; hence, no evil may appear in theft. If any nation saw no use in confirming the paternity of offspring, or had no desire for it, they might perceive no moral evil in practices which more civilized nations see as destructive to society. But no nation has yet been found to be indifferent to these matters.

<margin>Why it is necessary to consider the connection of virtue with interest.</margin>

# BOOK I. PART II.

## An Inquiry into the SUPREME HAPPINESS of MANKIND.

### CHAP. VI.

#### *How far the several Sensations, Appetites, Passions and Affections are in our power.*

<margin>*Wherein happiness consists.*</margin>
I. THE chief happiness of any being must consist in the full enjoyment of all the gratifications its nature desires and is capable of; or if its nature allows for a great variety of pleasures of different and sometimes inconsistent kinds—some of them also higher and more durable than others—its supreme happiness must consist in the most constant enjoyment of the more intense and durable pleasures, along with as much of the lower gratifications as is consistent with the full enjoyment of the higher ones. In like manner, if we cannot ward off all pain, and there are different kinds and degrees of it, we must protect ourselves against the more intense and durable kinds, and the higher degrees of them; and this is done sometimes by enduring the lower kinds or degrees, or by sacrificing some smaller pleasures when it is necessary for this end.

### CHAP. 6.

<image-desc>A decorative horizontal flourish consisting of two symmetrical wavy lines.</image-desc>

<margin>How we have power over our desires.</margin>
1. Just as the calm desires and dislikes of the soul naturally arise from our opinions of good or evil in their objects, so they are proportioned to the degrees of good or evil we perceive. We have power over the selfish desires for any particular good only by means of the calm original determination toward the greatest happiness, and by the power of reasoning and comparing, which may discover the values of the various objects of desire. It is by correcting our opinions of their values that the various desires are kept in their proper proportion. It is also by means of the other original determination toward public happiness of the most extensive kind, and by a similar exercise of reason in comparing the values of the objects desired for others, that we can regulate the various kind affections and desires; since where a greater good is discerned, the calm desire for it is stronger than the desire for a smaller, conflicting good, whether pursued for ourselves or for others.

Here too the *moral faculty* displays much of its power. As the various narrower affections may often interfere and oppose each other, or some of them may be inconsistent with more extensive affections toward whole societies or toward mankind, our *moral sense*—by its stronger and warmer approval of the more extensive interests—both points out the affection which should prevail and confirms this nobler affection through our natural desire for *moral excellence*.

### Book I.

<margin>
How we have power over the passions.
</margin>
The turbulent appetites and particular passions, whether of the selfish or generous kind, are governed by the same means. They naturally arise on certain occasions, and often with great vehemence. To govern and restrain them, a habit is necessary, which must be acquired by frequent reflection and discipline. While we are calm, we must frequently pay attention to the danger of following the first appearances of good or evil too hastily; we must recall our former experiences within ourselves and our observations of others: how superior and more lasting enjoyments have been lost by our hasty indulgence of some pressing appetite or passion; how lasting misery and remorse have followed some fleeting gratification; what shame, distress, and sorrow have been the effects of ungoverned anger; and what infamy and contempt men have brought upon themselves through excessive fear, or by their aversion to labor and strenuous application. We may thus cultivate a habitual suspicion of unexamined appearances and a habitual caution when we feel any turbulent passion arising. When the calm principles are thus strengthened by frequent meditation, and the force of the passions is reduced, it is then that we obtain true liberty and self-command: the calm powers will retain and exercise that authority for which their natural dignity has prepared them, and our reason will be exercised in correcting all appearances of good and evil, and examining the true importance of the several objects of our appetites or passions.

<margin>*Associations of ideas.*</margin>
3. But no cause of excessive desires or unfair evaluations is more frequent than some groundless associations of ideas, formed by education or our usual conversations. These link confused notions of happiness—and even of virtue and moral perfection, or their opposites—to things that have little connection to them. Objects of desire are rarely presented to the mind as they truly are, without some disguise. Wealth and power are truly useful, not only for the natural conveniences or pleasures of life, but as a resource for acts of kindness. However, many notions are also often attached to them regarding great abilities, wisdom, moral excellence, and much higher joys than they can actually provide. These ideas so intoxicate some men that they forget their natural purposes, begin to love wealth and power for their own sake, and strive for the ostentation of them. They dread lower social positions as degrading, miserable, and inconsistent with moral worth or honor. Some natural pleasures are also, through similar associations, valued far above their worth, and immoderate desires for them torment the soul.

<margin>Other desires are more difficult to gratify than the appetites.</margin>
It is more difficult to gratify other most uneasy desires, arising from certain opinions of great happiness in particular enjoyments. If we had formed no such opinions or confused notions, we would have felt no misery in the lack of these enjoyments; this is not the case with the appetites. But when we can change these opinions and rectify our confused imaginations, the desires and their attendant anxieties cease or diminish. A greater share of the misery of life is caused by these desires than by the appetites. Of this kind are the desires for wealth, power, the grandeur and elegance of living, and fame; and our aversions to their opposites are of the same nature. Our affections for others, and our kind desires, are affected by opinions in the same manner as our selfish ones. What we conceive as a great good, we must warmly desire for those we love; we must be uneasy upon any disappointment.

False notions of virtue may be less lasting than other mistakes. Persons injured by them seldom fail to remonstrate; spectators not blinded by our passions and interest will show their disgust. And thus our ill-grounded joy and self-approbation may soon give place to shame and remorse.

<margin>How our endeavors have some effect.</margin>
IX. As for other enjoyments which are uncertain: though pure, unmixed happiness is not attainable, yet our endeavors are not useless. We hinted already that having had high previous expectations—though it may increase the first transports of success when the preceding anxiety is removed—actually lessens the subsequent enjoyment, and further embitters disappointments, making misfortunes that are light in their own nature become unsupportable. So, having lower expectations about these uncertain objects and keeping our desires moderate actually increases our stable sense of pleasure in the object obtained and lessens the sense of disappointment.

Thus the temperate, the sober, the chaste, and the humble have senses at least as acute as others, and enjoy all the good in sensual objects and in honor. Abstinence and restraint, when virtue requires them, corrupts no sense or appetite. Moderation in prosperity, temperance, humility, and modesty, and having low notions of happiness in sensual objects do not prevent any sense of pleasure in advantages obtained. Men of this turn have their reason calm and active to procure the gratifications they desire, and to find out other preferable enjoyments when they are disappointed. <margin>Enjoyments are valued by their dignity and duration.</margin>As to pleasures of the same kind, it is manifest that their values are proportionate to both their intensity and duration. In estimating duration, we regard not only the constancy of the object—or its remaining in our power—and the duration of the sensations it affords, but also the constancy of our own taste or relish; for when this changes, it puts an end to the enjoyment.

In comparing pleasures of different kinds, the value depends on both the duration and the dignity of the kind together. We have an immediate sense of a <note>See above, chapter 4, section 10.</note> dignity, a perfection, or a beatific quality in some kinds, which no intensity of the lower kinds can equal, even if they were as lasting as we could wish. No intensity or duration of any external sensation gives it a dignity or worth equal to that of the improvement of the soul through knowledge or the fine arts; and much less is it equal to that of virtuous affections and actions. We never hesitate in judging the happiness or perfection of others in this way, provided that the impetuous cravings of appetites and passions do not corrupt our judgments, as they often do in our own case. By this intimate feeling of dignity, enjoyments and exercises of some kinds—though not of the highest degree of those kinds—are incomparably more excellent and beatific than the most intense and lasting enjoyments of the lower kinds. ...with sufficient duration may complete our happiness; it may be more convenient to estimate enjoyments by their dignity and duration: dignity denoting the excellence of the kind, when those of different kinds are compared; and the intensity of the sensations, when we compare those of the same kind.

<margin>The different tastes of men.</margin>
II. Although the several original powers mentioned above are natural to all men, yet through habit, associated ideas, education, or opinion, some generally pursue enjoyments of one kind and show a disregard for others which are highly valued by men of a different disposition. Some are much given to sensuality; others to more ingenious pleasures; others pursue wealth and power; others moral and social enjoyments, and honor. Wealth and power have a few faithful followers adoring them for their own sake; but the more numerous worshipers adore them only as ministering spirits, or mediators with some superior divinities, such as *pleasure, honor, and beneficence*.

<margin>These must be examined.</margin>
Thus different men have different tastes. What one admires as the supreme enjoyments, another may despise. Must we not examine these tastes? Are all persons, all orders of beings, equally happy if each obtains the enjoyments they respectively relish most? At this rate, the meanest brute or insect may be as happy as the wisest hero, patriot, or friend can be. What may make a brute as happy as that low order is capable of being may be but despicable to an order endowed with finer perceptive powers and a nobler sort of desires. Beings of these higher orders are immedi-

Nature has thus distinguished the different orders by different perceptive powers, so that the same objects will not be sufficient for happiness to all; nor do all have equal happiness even when each can gratify all the desires and senses he has.

The superior orders in this world probably experience all the sensations of the lower orders and can judge them. But the inferior do not experience the enjoyments of the superior. Indeed, in the several stages of life, each person finds different tastes and desires. We are conscious in our mature years that the happiness of our friends, our families, or our country are incomparably nobler objects of our pursuit, and provide a proportionally nobler pleasure than the toys which once entertained us abundantly when we had experienced nothing better. God has assigned to each order, and to the several stages of life in the same person, their peculiar powers and tastes. Each is as happy when its taste is gratified as it can then be. But we are immediately conscious that one gratification is more excellent than another when we have experienced both. And then our reason and observation enable us to compare the effects, consequences, and duration. One may be transitory and the cause of great subsequent misery, though for the present the enjoyment is intense; another may be lasting, safe, and followed by no satiety, shame, disgust, or remorse.

<margin>What men are the best judges.</margin>
Superior beings, by more divine faculties and fuller knowledge, may—without experience of all sorts—immediately discern which are the noblest. They may have some intuitive knowledge of perfection and some standard for it, which may make the experience of some lower sorts useless to them. But among mankind, those are certainly the best judges who have full experience, with their tastes, senses, and appetites in a naturally vigorous state. Now, it has never been alleged that social affections, the admiration of moral excellence, the desire for esteem (with their attendant and guardian, temperance), the pursuits of knowledge, or natural activity ever impaired any sense or appetite. This is often charged, with great justice, against luxury, overindulgence, and indolence. The highest sensual enjoyments may be experienced by those who employ both mind and body vigorously in social, virtuous duties, and allow all the natural appetites to return in their proper seasons. Such people are certainly the best judges of all enjoyments. Thus, according to the maxim often emphasized by Aristotle, “The good man is the true judge and standard of everything.”

<margin>The vicious can seldom judge well.</margin>

<margin>
Sensual pleasures are the lowest.
</margin>
The pleasures of the external senses are of two classes: those of the palate and those between the sexes. We call both of these sensual.

<margin>
Those of the palate.
</margin>
The pleasures of the palate, no matter how pleasing they may be to children, must appear the lowest and most insignificant enjoyments to all thoughtful people who have experienced any others. The discomfort felt when the body needs nourishment may be quite intense, as it is wisely designed to prompt us to take necessary care of the body. Relieving this pain may give a strong sensation of pleasure at first. But the actual pleasure of taste—the direct enjoyment—must be insignificant to all who are above the level of animals. The differences in pleasure among the various kinds of food are so small that the sharpness of appetite is acknowledged to make a much greater difference. Imagine a life spent in this enjoyment without interruption, and that, contrary to the present order of nature, the appetite still remained; but that there was no social enjoyment or affection, no finer perceptions, or exercise of the intellectual powers. This state is lower than that of many animals. Their appetites allow intervals for some pleasures of a social nature and for action; and when thus employed, they show a higher joy than in feeding.

The short duration.

The duration of these sensations is also insignificant. Such indeed is the bounty of *God* that the means of satisfying the cravings of appetite may be easily obtained; and thus, by good management, we may all frequently enjoy almost the highest pleasures of this kind. But the appetite is soon satisfied and does not return until after long intervals. Artificial incentives may create an unnatural craving, but the satisfying of this gives little pleasure. It is a real depravity and sickness; and, when continued for a long time, it turns into such a physical ailment that it must stop all enjoyments. Where grandeur and variety are sought after, the imagination grows capricious and inconstant, and the objects of desire become uncertain. This inclination may become too expensive for our wealth and increase even while the means of satisfying it are diminished.

<margin>Sensual enjoyments consistent with virtue are as high as any.</margin>
It is also proper to observe here that not all sensual gratifications are opposed to moral enjoyments. There is a moderate indulgence that is perfectly innocent and sufficient to satisfy the unease of appetite; which, through wise economy, can often be as high as any sort of sensual enjoyment, and even contribute to moral ones. The temperate, and those who—after proper self-government in celibacy—have made a wise choice in marriage, may have as high sensual enjoyments as any. In recommending virtue, we do not need to assume it is opposed to all gratifications of the senses, though its power in our hearts should be maintained at such a high level that it is able to control all the appetites that might happen to oppose it. Its gentle sway generally allows for gratifications that may be the highest of their kind; or where it does not, it makes abundant compensation for the loss through the joyful approval of such abstinence and self-government. What rich compensation is made by the joyful approval one must feel for fidelity, friendship, and deserving well, and by the returns of a constant affection from a worthy heart, to make up for the lack of irregular, shameful, perplexing, and joyless passions and indulgences with people of no moral worth or steadiness of affection.

VI. Pleasures of the sympathetic kind, arising from the fortunes of others, are proportional to the strength of the kind affections we have for them. Our nature is exceedingly susceptible to these affections, especially the stronger types of them toward offspring, parents, kinsmen, benefactors, or eminently worthy characters, as well as toward sects, parties, and countries. They provide the far greater part of the activity, and of the happiness or misery of life.

All that we can do to secure any fund of joys of this kind is to examine well the merit of persons and causes, and by these means to turn our stronger affections toward the superior merit of men of true goodness and correct imaginations, whose happiness is less inconstant than that of others; to have a firm persuasion of the wisdom and goodness of providence, and to cultivate the most extensive affections. The stronger our universal good-will is, if our joys are so much higher upon general prosperity, the greater also will our regret be upon perceived general misery. But what makes this affection always safe in all events, and a fund of superior joy, is a firm persuasion of a good Providence governing the universe for the best, amid all the apparent evils and disorders. Of this more hereafter.

<margin>In respect of dignity.</margin>
How much inferior are the highest sensual pleasures, or even those of the imagination or speculative knowledge, compared to the stable joy of a conscious goodness of heart; and to that high approval one feels for oneself in any important duties for the good of one’s country or friend; and to the joyful thought of deserving well of mankind and earning their applause? Kind affections alone sit easily in the heart; there is an inward satisfaction in them, and we joyfully maintain them for life. <note>This is often justly observed by Aristotle and Cicero.</note> But our nature is fitted for more than inactive affection. A high happiness arises from exercising our powers; and the nobler the power is, the more blissful is its exercise. When virtuous efforts are successful, there is such a collection of pure joys from conscious goodness, sympathy with others, and the expected love and approval of all—especially the satisfaction of our Maker—that it far surpasses all other enjoyments. <margin>These pleasures are most lasting.</margin>
The idea here is not inconsistent. Our taste for virtue increases through practice, and habits make it even more pleasant. The memory of it is always delightful and makes the enjoyment lasting, provided there are correct ideas of virtue and of the merit of the people and causes involved. One goal proposed in the creation of different orders of beings, and in the ordaining of different states for those of the same species—some more and some less perfect—is likely this: that nobler minds should never lack opportunities for the joyful exercise of their good intentions toward those who are inferior either in their perfection or their circumstances. These joys, too, are placed beyond the power of fortune as long as men remain of sound mind. A humble status, a difficult life, or external disadvantages may prevent us from providing the most important services to others in material ways; however, these can neither hinder the healthy inward affections of the heart nor a course of action suited to our abilities, and this is the highest virtue.

<margin>Correct ideas of virtue are necessary.</margin>
Unexamined admiration of some partial moral forms, and some narrow affections, without true ideas of merit in people and causes, may lead us into conduct that, upon better information, may become a source of shame and remorse. But where, through close reflection, we have attained correct ideas of virtue and merit, and of the effective means of doing good, virtuous action—as it is the natural purpose of a rational and

<margin>Pleasures of honor are very intense.</margin>
IX. The pleasures of honor—arising from the approval, esteem, and gratitude of others—as they naturally follow from virtue, so when they are founded on it, are among the most pleasing feelings of the soul. These joys of honor and virtue, and sympathetic joys, are naturally connected, nor do we need to compare them in detail; since the same conduct naturally serves them all: and where they coincide, no words can express the happiness enjoyed. Sympathetic feelings may be more intense in some tender, affectionate hearts; active spirits in public positions may be more affected by conscious virtue and earned glory. But where these three are united, with a firm persuasion of a good *God* approving our character and ensuring universal order and happiness, our state must come nearest to *that joy unspeakable and full of glory* which we hope for as the perfect fulfillment of our rational nature.

<margin>And of great duration.</margin>
True glory is also durable, unlike sensual enjoyments, which pass like the shadow of a cloud, leaving no trace behind them. The approval and esteem of others, when founded on virtue, will likely continue throughout life and survive after us; and the approval of God shall be everlasting. The pursuit of widespread fame for eminent abilities and virtues may indeed be subject to disappointment, be full of labor, and be liable to excess. Ordinary virtues, or even the highest virtues in humble positions, will not obtain the widespread applause of nations. But a wise and virtuous man may generally obtain such honor, whether in a narrow or broad sphere, as to provide great joy. And a good heart, persuaded of a kind providence observing all things, is sure of the approval of the best judge, and that for eternity.

<margin>The pleasures of mirth are on the side of virtue.</margin>
X. Among such solemn subjects, the pleasures of mirth and gaiety must be of small account. And yet even children despise sensuality in comparison to them; and sensual enjoyments borrow many of their charms from them, without which they would be despicable and shameful. They are an agreeable seasoning to other enjoyments and provide some relief from the fatigues of serious business. The nobler joys are grave, severe, and solemn. But human life must have relaxations. Now, whatever value we put upon mirth and gaiety, it must be placed on the side of virtue: since a mind is always best disposed to receive all cheerfulness and pleasantry when it is kind and at ease, free from anger, ill-will, envy, or remorse. <margin>Wealth and power are more blissful for the virtuous than for others.</margin>
As wealth and power are not immediately pleasant, but are the means of obtaining pleasures, their importance to happiness must be in proportion to that of the enjoyments to which they are directed by the possessor. The virtuous man, therefore, who directs them toward generous and virtuous purposes, has a much nobler enjoyment of them than those who direct them toward the pleasures of the imagination or the elegance of life; and yet this is a finer application than that of sensuality. Where, through confused imaginations, they are not directly applied to their natural purposes but are pursued for themselves, avarice and ambition become wretched, insatiable cravings, hateful to all mankind; and the possessions become joyless to the person who obtains them.

<margin>Such passions are not useless in our nature.</margin>
These passions of the unkind sort are not useless parts of our nature. Upon the perception of injury or damage done to us, or to those we love, anger naturally arises to rouse us for defense. When persons we do not respect are preferred over those of higher merit, an honest concern and indignation arises. A similar indignation arises against all those who appear grossly immoral. Indulgence may make these passions strong and habitual. The feelings attending them are inherent uneasiness and torment; however, for the general good, it was reasonable that we should be subjected to them to some degree on certain occasions, just as we are to bodily pain. Even the sweetest tempers have experienced short fits of them and have felt how uneasily these moments pass. Where such passions are intense and lasting, degenerating into rancor and settled malice and envy, the misery must be very great; it is no wonder, then, that the removal of it should at first give considerable pleasure. <margin>Our moral sense values affections and enjoyments in proportion to their tendency toward the general good.</margin>

Consider cases, as in some ancient fables, where—based on such false information that only a flawed, passionate, impetuous, and cruel temper could have believed it—someone had tortured to death an unknown person, who is afterward found to have been their tender parent, their dutiful son, their generous friend, or their affectionate brother. <margin>CHAPTER 7.</margin>
Who could wish a son or friend to be instead sunk irrecoverably in all vice and baseness of soul, yet free from pain and abounding with sensual pleasures; rather than exposed to the greatest tortures in some act of heroism, with a lively sense of integrity and self-esteem, and the sympathetic joys in the prosperity of every interest that is dear to him?

The natural strength of the human mind in resisting pain would appear much greater, were it not for the terrors of death which generally attend the severer kinds of it. Remove this fear, and the soul can bear it much more easily. In some diversions, and in the accidents which attend them, where there is no fear of anything fatal, men without dejection of mind—nay, sometimes with gaiety—can bear very acute pain, and despise it. <note>On this subject many noble sentiments are to be found in *Cicero’s Tusculan Disputations, Book II*.</note>

<margin>Bodily pain may be very lasting.</margin>
Pain in the extremities of the body may be very lasting. But all bodily pain differs from moral feelings in this: it leaves no sense of evil when the uneasy sensation ceases. The reflection on it is pleasant rather than uneasy, when there is no fear of its returning. The soul is often bettered by it, as experience gives it more strength and fortitude. Where pain was endured in any honorable cause, it always remains a matter of joy and glory.

<margin>The sympathetic and moral pains the highest of all.</margin>
XV. The sympathetic and moral pain of remorse and infamy are the highest our nature admits, just as their opposite joys are the highest: they can make life quite intolerable. The misery of a beloved person, while it continues and is attended to, is incessant pain to the observer. When it ceases by death, the painful remembrance survives for a long time in an affectionate heart, until business diverts the thoughts or deep reflection suggests consolations. The sure refuge in such cases is in a good providence and that future happiness provided for all worthy objects of kind affections.

<margin>Why we are prone to tragic sights.</margin>
It is vain to allege that all sympathy carries with it pleasure superior to the pain. We would not then be inclined to change the state of the object. It is true we are prone to run to spectacles of misery and are fond of tragedies; and yet, misery alone observed is the cause of misery only. But there is a natural impulse, implanted for the kindest reasons, forcing us to such spectacles of misery, which generally brings relief to the sufferers. And we can restrain this impulse where we foresee that it can do no good. Let no one be surprised by such impulses where no pleasure is in view, or any removal of our own pain: do we not observe after the death of a dear friend, when we can serve him no more, nor enjoy any sympathetic pleasures with him, that the tormenting thoughts of his dying agonies and groans recur to our minds for many weeks, and months, and years. <margin>The delights in tragedy.</margin>In tragedy, there is a vivid imitation of behavior and heroic virtues struggling against fortune, and noble sentiments and affections are expressed. <header>the several TEMPERS.</header>

## CHAP. 8.

<margin>All our affections are useful in the system.</margin>
As all the senses and affections mentioned above are parts of our internal makeup, so each of them has its natural use either to the individual itself, or to the system of which it is a part. Moral goodness indeed consists principally in the social and kind affections carrying us out beyond ourselves. But there is a natural usefulness in the private or selfish affections, while they are kept within certain bounds, not only to the good of the individual, but to that of the system; nor is any one complete in his nature without them. And as the happiness of a system results from that of the individuals, it is necessary to it that each one has the selfish affections in that degree which his best state requires, consistently with his most effective services to the public.

<margin>The best constitution of a species.</margin>
The most benign and wise constitution of a rational system is that in which the degree of selfish affection most useful to the individual is consistent with the interest of the system; and where the degree of generous affections most useful to the system is ordinarily consistent with or conducive to the greatest happiness of the individual. A mean, low species may indeed be wholly subjected to the interests of a superior species, and have affections solely calculated for these higher interests. But in the more noble systems it would be a flaw if in fact there was an established inconsistency between the two grand ends for each rational being—personal enjoyment and public happiness—and consequently, an irreconcilable variance between the affections destined for the pursuit of them.

<summary>This page explains that both social and selfish affections are necessary components of human nature, serving both the individual and the broader social system. It argues that in a well-ordered rational system, personal happiness and the public good should be naturally consistent rather than in conflict.</summary>

<margin>No natural affection is absolutely evil.</margin>
None of our affections can be called absolutely evil in every degree; and yet a certain high degree, beyond the proportion of the rest—even in some of our generous affections—may be vicious, or at least a great imperfection, detrimental both to the individual and the system. At the same time, the greatest strength of any one kind is not of itself necessarily evil: indeed, it may be innocent if the other affections have a strength proportioned to this kind, and to the dignity of their several natures and of the purposes for which they were implanted. But where the mind is not capacious enough to contain this high degree of other affections, any one of the selfish affections, and many of the generous ones, may be excessive. Calm, extensive goodwill, the desire for moral excellence, the love of God, and resignation to his will can never exceed: as they do not exclude any partial good affection as far as it is useful, nor any just regard for private good. But the more confined affections, even of the generous sort, may exceed their due proportion and exclude or overpower other affections of a better sort: as we often see in parental love, pity, party-zeal, *etc.* The <term>moral turpitude</term> consists not in the strength of these affections, but in the weakness of the more extensive ones in proportion to their dignity and superior use.

<margin>The evil consists in a lack of proportion.</margin>

<margin>Restraining the social affections is immoral and harmful.</margin>
To root out or diminish the social affections, even if it would prevent or diminish our social sorrows, must also destroy or diminish proportionally all our social and most of our moral joys. The reduction of even the narrower affections is rather a detriment to the human character. The most natural and perfect state of which our minds currently seem capable is that where all the natural affections, desires, and senses are preserved vigorously, in proportion to the dignity of the object they pursue; so that the inferior are still kept under the restraint of the superior, and never allowed to defeat the end for which God intended them; or to control either of the two grand determinations of our souls toward the happiness and perfection of the individual, and that of the <term>system</term>.

<margin>
These are not absolutely evil in all degrees.

We have established names for the excesses of these unkind passions—or when they arise without just or proportional causes and are habitual—namely, *malice*, *revenge*, *envy*, *ambition*, or *pride*. But we have no such settled names for their innocent degrees. Hence, some have too rashly imagined that some of our natural passions are absolutely evil in all degrees.

But these unkind passions, though uncomfortable even while innocent, were implanted partly for the interest of the individual and partly for that of the system. Just as the external senses, through pleasant perceptions, point out the safe state of the body and ordinary enjoyments to the individual, and rouse him on the other hand by uncomfortable sensations occasionally to ward off what is destructive; so the *moral faculty*, in a similar service to the public, recommends all kind affections and actions to the agent (and to every observer as well) through a pleasant approval. On the other hand, through uncomfortable reluctance and remorse, it deters the agent from such affections as are harmful to the system, and through the uncomfortable impulses of anger and indignation, it rouses every observer to oppose his designs.

Now, just as a sense or appetite is corrupted in an individual when it loathes its natural food or craves what is not nourishing—or as the organs of feeling must be disordered and sickly when they are pained by healthy air or necessary clothing—surely that disposition of mind must be just as corrupted when anger arises without any hurt or injury being received; or aversion and hatred where there is no moral evil in the object; or envy at the success of merit; or ill will toward any innocent part of a system formed for, and preserved by, a social life and an exchange of good deeds.

It is therefore in our interest to examine carefully the merit of persons and causes, and to keep a tight rein over the unkind passions, which are uncomfortable even when they are innocent. They are so prone to excess that, even in their moderate degrees, they look so much like something evil that they are rarely approved of. The calmer affections of the soul toward the good of either the individual or the system are generally more effective than the turbulent passions, whatever use these passions may have in minds not accustomed to reflection. It is desirable, therefore, to have our lives guided by these safer guides and to maintain a habitual caution against all violent

<margin>*Two types of imperfections incident to our kind affections;*</margin>
IV. If the social affections are, in themselves and their consequences, the noblest enjoyments, it is plain that the calm and extensive ones are the best of that kind, when they are in their full vigor and enjoy their natural authority to direct or restrain the various narrower affections.

Two imperfections are incident to our kind affections: one is when they extend only to a part of mankind, and yet without any bad dispositions toward any other part; the other is where, in the course of the operation of strong, kind, partial affections toward some, unkind and mischievous affections are likely to be excited toward others.

<margin>*not of full extent,*</margin>
In the first case, people of less reflection may never form that most diffused, calm purpose or desire for the good of all, which is the highest moral excellence; and yet they may have friendly dispositions as far as their views and sphere of action extend, without ill will toward anyone. This temperament is very excellent, nor can more be expected from the generality of mankind; nor is more necessary, as very few have the power to perform the most extensive services. It is no unjust partiality when people generally follow the stronger ties of nature, or the bonds of gratitude, or the impulses of hearty esteem toward their worthy friends—provided they neglect no such duties as occur toward others, and can restrain these narrower affections when they are opposite to any more extensive interest which they discover.

<margin>Chapter 8. *or unjustly partial.*</margin>
Dangerous partiality occurs when there are strong affections for a few, without any regard for other parts of the system that are equally valuable and within the range of our knowledge and sphere of action; or, perhaps, when there are malicious dispositions toward them without natural causes, or quite out of proportion to those causes, or without any benefit to the public interest. These social, though partial, affections are often sources of pleasure; but the aversions may create just as much unease. When kind affections are directed so capriciously, there is little merit in them; they must be inconsistent, and self-approval must vanish upon reflection. The object now admired may soon be disliked and abhorred, driven by the same capriciousness that made it agreeable. In these partial affections, there is less shared joy; and what merit is there in love without a proportionate cause? What satisfaction is there in receiving love from favorites who were chosen unwisely? Whereas universal goodwill, and even limited affections based on natural causes—which do not exclude just affection toward others—must be full of joy and provide the consciousness of deserving well from everyone, as such affections serve the good of all.

<margin>*Danger of ill-grounded aversions.*</margin>
Unjust aversions arising from a misguided conscience and false notions of religion and virtue, formed by superstition and poor education, must lead to innumerable inconsistencies. If men do not banish all reflection, there must be grievous remorse and inward displeasure: a bigot, a persecutor, or a robber, with a sort of conscience regarding his duty to his party or his system

What value are services to a party or cause when we have no true conviction of its worth, and when they are in opposition to the interests of many others? What satisfaction is there in pleasing a demon of whose moral perfections we can have no accurate or consistent idea? The struggles must be terrible between all the principles of humanity and this false conscience. Reflection must always raise torturing suspicions that everything is wrong. All stable satisfaction must be lost; or else one must banish reason and inquiry.

Upon a false point of honor, one might kill a friend. Compassion and remorse immediately follow. In persecution too, or cruelty resulting from party zeal, might not the protests of the sufferers, the talk of the world, or the words of the persecuted party raise inward horrors and remorse, even where they are often boldly denied? What is it like to offend multitudes and to be abhorred by them? How hard is it to justify any conduct that is contrary to humanity? What will our condition be in later, calmer years, when our present ambition and party spirit may fade, and we shall see that our conduct was full of guilt and cruelty toward the innocent, and offensive to God and all wise men? A good mind will never think it can be too cautious against any such superstitions or party prejudices that may embitter it against any of its fellow creatures.

<margin>Ambition is miserable.</margin>
The same things may be said regarding the desires for power and glory. A moderate degree is innocent and useful; but when these desires become too violent, they are restless and distressing to the individual, often harmful to society, and generally break through the most sacred ties of duty and humanity, ruining every good disposition of the heart. To desire a reputation for integrity and moral worth is natural to every good character; it motivates people to become what they wish to be known as, which is the shortest path to true glory. Indeed, the desire for excellence in valuable skills, while it is moderate, is a useful and innocent part of our nature. But it can become so intense that it becomes a constant torment and the source of the most despicable and miserable passions. Any superior merit in others will then provoke envy, ill-will, and a tendency toward belittling others. The mind will become restless, violent, jealous, fault-finding, easily provoked, unable to bear the slightest neglect, distressing to everyone, and disliked by all. No passion can undermine its own goal more than vanity; just as nothing is more hateful and contemptible than arrogance, nothing is more lovely than its opposite: modesty and humility.

Thus, the excesses of the selfish passions are certain misery. They constitute the character called *selfish*, which is despicable and deprived of all the nobler joys of life. Because this temperament is shameful, it leads to subtle conduct and feigned behavior; it loses its natural frankness and candor, and acquires distrust, suspicion, and envy. A self-interest separate from our fellows is formed more and more every day, and social impulses are suppressed. At last, the temperament becomes completely wretched and hateful.

<margin>*Tyranny.*</margin>

<margin>Savage cruelty.</margin>
Civilized nations of great humanity, based on false conceptions of the spirit and tempers of the rest of mankind, and from some absurd notions of dignity and pre-eminence in themselves, have thought others fit only to be slaves. Some have found such entertainment from the surprising efforts of skill and courage that, insensitive to the misery which was obvious to their sight every moment, they considered it a spectacle of high delight to behold gladiators putting each other to death. We all know the notions held by the common people concerning all heretics; we know the pride of schoolmen and many ecclesiastics—how it irritates their insolent vanity that any man should presume to be wiser than they are in religious tenets by differing from them. When this insolent pride is long indulged by the enjoyment of power and popular veneration, it grows enormous; and it may explain how such men, and their implicit followers, can behold with joy the most horrific tortures of men who are truly innocent, but portrayed in all the forms of impiety and wickedness. It is unnecessary to explain the origin of other monstrous dispositions.

<margin>From the structures of animal bodies;</margin>

This wondrous structure appearing, not in a few instances, but in every one of the innumerable individuals of each species; similar to each other in their structures, and endowed with the several powers and instincts of their kind, for their preservation and the continuance of the species. What precise organs to distinguish, receive, grind, swallow, and digest their food; and to diffuse the nourishment to all their parts! what a variety and precise structure of organs for spontaneous motions, subservient to their pleasure, support, or defense!

<margin>Connection of the sun and atmosphere with the earth and animal bodies.</margin>
III. The earth and all its beauties depend on the sun. It is placed at the most convenient distance: <gloss>a</gloss> a considerably nearer or more distant situation would make it a less convenient habitation. The eyes of animals are fitted to the degree of light and to their proper occupations with the most admirable art; stronger light would be painful and harmful, and fainter would be inconvenient. Their lungs, their ears, and their blood are suited to the surrounding air, its weight, and its ordinary motions. This yielding, pressing, beneficial fluid is the means of life, of breathing, of the circulation of blood, of the voice to communicate desires and sentiments, and of gratifying their taste for harmony.

Such is the extent of the ocean, which is itself also full of inhabitants suited to that element; such is the heat of the sun, that vast quantities of vapors, freed of their salts, are daily raised and float in the air until, having grown too dense, they descend in fruitful showers; or, meeting with hills or mountains in their motion, they are condensed and feed springs and rivers, which, after carrying water to great tracts of land, are again discharged into the ocean. Thus all is full of power, activity, and regular motion, wisely and exquisitely adapted to the uses of the living and sentient parts of the creation.

<margin>The art of men or other visible agents is not the cause of these things.</margin>
IV. The several classes of plants and animals owe none of this wondrous structure to any wisdom of their own or that of their parents; no art of theirs contrived the physical frame, the internal structure of their powers and instincts, or the conveniences of their habitat. This immense power and wisdom must reside elsewhere, in some other being. Even if the world were supposed to be eternal, the argument remains the same. The effects—the evidences of wisdom—were, upon that supposition, present at all times. In all times, therefore, wisdom and power superior to the human have existed in some other being. If this admirable structure had a beginning, the evidence is even more manifest.

### BOOK I.

<margin>Apparent contradictions arise from ignorance.</margin>
Observe all of nature as far as our knowledge extends; we find its design to be good. The objections of the *Epicureans* and of some *moderns* arose from their ignorance. The alleged blemishes are now known to be either the unavoidable accompaniments or consequences of a structure and laws that serve advantages which far outweigh these inconveniences; or sometimes they are the direct and natural means of obtaining these advantages. The vast ocean, often thought to be barren, we find is a necessary reservoir of water for the use of all land animals; it is also populated with its own tribes and richly supplied for their survival, from which men also derive great support. The mountains are useful partly for pasture, fruits, and grain, and partly for producing rain, springs, and rivers. Storms arise from the very causes most necessary for life: the sun's evaporation of water and the movement of these vapors in the air. The care, attention, and labor required of men for their survival invigorate both the soul and the body. Without them, the earth becomes a barren forest; but through them, it becomes a joyful and abundant home. These efforts are the natural causes of health and wisdom. It is in every way to our advantage that we have no such lazy paradise as the poets imagined in the golden age.*

Some authors ask, "Why are we made of such poor materials that we are often oppressed with pain during life; often tormented by our own passions, and by the injuries of others? Our frame too at last decays, and we yield our places with great pain to our successors of the same species. Why are we made of such frail materials? Why this succession of generations? Why are our minds so imperfect, either in knowledge or virtue? Might we not have had a greater strength of understanding, and a better balance among our affections?"

<margin>
Different orders necessary in the best system.
</margin>
In answer to these difficult questions, let us consider what is highly probable: that the best possible constitution of an immense system of perceptive beings may necessarily require a diversity of orders, some higher in perfection and happiness, and some lower. There may be abundant enjoyments for some orders of beings without social action. But we are sure of this from experience: that there are orders of beings quite high in the scale whose supreme enjoyments consist in kind affections, and in exerting their powers in good deeds arising from these affections. Indeed, it is impossible for us to conceive of a higher sort of enjoyment. The consciousness of goodwill toward others, even if inactive, is highly delightful; but there is still a superior joy in practicing this disposition through beneficent actions. What if this is the supreme enjoyment in nature, as our minds seem to feel it is? This would be excluded from nature in a great measure, unless there were imperfection, poverty, pain, and even moral evil in nature.

<margin>Experience of evil gives a higher sense of good and exercises virtue.</margin>

The whole life of virtue among men, which we showed to be the chief enjoyment, is a combat with natural or moral evils. No place can be found for liberality where there is no poverty; or for fortitude where there is no danger; or for temperance where there are no lower appetites and passions; or for mercy and forgiveness, or friendly admonitions and counsels, and long-suffering, and the returning of good for evil, where a species is incapable of moral evil. Such lovely duties, the remembrance of which must be eternally delightful, must be excluded, or some moral evils must exist. Indeed, what patience, resignation, and trust in God can be exercised in a system where misery cannot exist? If, then, the highest enjoyments we can conceive are fit to be introduced into the universe, some evils must accompany them. Furthermore, how can we conceive of the life of the highest orders of beings if there were none inferior to them; no good to be done, no kind acts, no evils to be warded off, or good formerly lacking to be shared? <margin>No effect from two opposite principles.</margin>
Opposite intentions in *two causes* of equal skill and power could have no effect. They could have no motive to unite in forming a world, since each would know that the skill and power of the other would introduce as much of what was offensive to him as his own skill or power could achieve of what was agreeable.

Upon this supposition, should we not plainly observe malicious mechanisms in the works of nature as frequently as we observe those that are kind and useful? But nothing of this sort occurs. No malice—original, steady, and unprovoked—appears in the works of nature; but on many occasions we see kindness that is gratuitous and unmerited: in the tender relations of life, in the esteem we hold for virtuous characters by whom we have not benefited, and in compassion toward the unknown. There is no original or natural joy in misery; it never pleases us without some previous notion of great moral evil in the sufferer, or some opposition to our own interest. No *moral faculty* is observed approving of what is hurtful to the public; but in all rational agents, we find a contrary faculty, which immediately approves of all kindness,

The case, however, is otherwise. Happiness is far superior to misery, even in this present world; and this completes all the evidence we could expect or require.

<margin>Histories give us a view of only a small part of life.</margin>
While histories relate wars, rebellions, massacres, and the corruptions and intrigues of courts, they are silent about those vastly superior numbers who, in safe obscurity, are virtuously or innocently employed in the natural business and enjoyments of mankind. We read the actions of the great—of men exposed to all the temptations of greed and ambition, raised above the common lot of honest labor and industry, with minds often corrupted from their infancy by the elevation of their fortunes, and all their passions inflamed by flattery and luxury. The social, joyful, innocent employments of the bulk of mankind are not subjects of history; nor even the ordinary, regular administration of a state in the protection of a people and the execution of justice. Histories dwell upon critical times, the sicknesses of states, the parties, factions, and their contentions, revolutions, foreign wars, and their causes. These dangers, their causes, and the remedies applied must be recorded for the use of future ages; and their rarity, in comparison to the natural business of social life, makes them more entertaining. In the same way, medical authors do not record the agreeable enjoyments and exercises of health. The causes, symptoms, and prognoses of disorders, their critical turns, and the effects of different medicines applied are the proper subjects of their dissertations.

<margin>If *God* is good, he is *perfectly* good.</margin>

If God is omnipotent and wise, all is well: the best order prevails throughout the whole. No evil is permitted which is not necessary for a superior good, or the necessary accompaniment and consequence of what is ordered with the most kind intention for the greatest perfection and happiness of the universe.

Five affections and a *moral faculty* make all orders of being endowed with them capable of incomparably greater happiness or misery than any of the brute kinds. If the duration of humans is to be eternal, and a happy immortality is obtained by these very means which are most beatific to us in this life, the evils of these few years during our mortal state are not worthy of regard; they are not even to be compared with the happiness to follow.

<margin>
No proofs to the contrary.
The soul seems distinct from matter.
</margin>

The boldest *Epicurean* never attempted direct proof that a future state is impossible. Many have believed it who conceived the soul to be material. Mankind in all ages and nations has hoped for it, without any prejudice of the senses in its favor. The opinion is natural to mankind, and is what their Creator designed they should entertain. It is confirmed not a little by arguments which show the subject of thought, reason, and affections not to be a divisible system of distinct substances, as every part of matter is. The simplicity and unity of consciousness could not result from modes dispersed and inherent in a collection of different bodies in distinct places.* Nor is the activity of the soul consistent with the passivity of matter. <margin>The nature of our perception confirms it.</margin>
The nature and order of our perceptions show this distinction. First, *external sensations* present forms quite distinct from this *self*, and no further related to it than that they are perceived. Their changes for better or worse do not affect or alter the state of the perceiver. A second set of perceptions approaches a little nearer: those of *bodily pleasure* and *pain*. The state of the *perceiving self* is affected by them, and made easy or uneasy. But *nature* ordains in a way quite inexplicable that these perceptions are connected with parts of the body, or the spaces which they once occupied; and the accident is naturally conceived as affecting the body, and not altering the dignity of the soul. Let *Anatomists* talk of motions propagated by nerves to the brain, or to some gland that is the seat of the soul: when the finger is cut, as surely as pain is felt at all, it is felt in the finger, or in the space where the finger was. *Nature* declares the event to be an accident to the body, not destroying or reducing the excellence of the perceiver—not even when the sensations indicate such accidents as must soon destroy the body altogether. Indeed, some such sensations of pain rather increase personal dignity, and some sensations of pleasure reduce it. But there is a third sort of perceptions, when we are conscious of knowledge, goodness, faith, integrity, friendliness, contempt for sensual pleasures, and public spirit. These we feel to be the immediate qualities of this *self*, the personal ex-

Virtue in many instances is beaten down and defeated in this world. There is no lack of power in *God*; no envy or ill-nature. Should one behold a building not yet finished, the several parts showing exquisite art, yet still wanting a further part to make all complete and convenient, with room left for this part and even some indications of this further building intended; would not an unbiased spectator conclude that this further part was also in the plan of the architect, though some reasons retarded the execution of it? This is the case in the moral world. The structure is exquisite, but not complete: we see space for further building and indications of the design in the desires and hopes of all ages and nations, in our natural sense of justice, and in our most noble and extensive affections concerning the state of others and of the universe; and shall we not trust and hope in the art, the goodness, and the inexhaustible wealth of the *great Architect*?

We have dwelt long on this subject, rather pointing out the sources of evidence than displaying it fully, because ascertaining the goodness of *God* is the grand foundation of our happiness and the main pillar of virtue. We shall briefly touch upon his other attributes, lest any mistakes about them should diminish that high veneration and admiration due to his excellence.

<margin>Chapter 9.</margin>
<margin>The other attributes of God. A spirit.</margin>
XVI. First, all the reasons which prove any thinking being to be a distinct substance from matter prove that *God* is a spirit, and is not the great material mass of this universe; as all the proofs of his existence are proofs of original thought, wisdom, consciousness, activity, and affection—powers quite inconsistent with the nature of matter. By calling him a spirit, we do not mean that he must be a substance of the same species or kind as the human soul, and only greater. Though all thinking beings differ in kind from all matter, yet there may be innumerable orders or kinds of spirits, with essential differences from each other, from that lowest spirit of life which is in the lowliest animal, to the *infinite Deity*.

<margin>Infinite.</margin>
Furthermore, what is *original* and *uncaused* cannot be conceived as limited in its nature—either by its own choice or by the will of any prior cause—to any particular finite degree of perfection, or to those of one kind while it lacks others. No possible reason or cause can be assigned for it having some types or degrees rather than others. We see from the effects that the original perfections are high beyond imagination; and there was no prior will or choice of any being to confine it to one species or degree. This leads us to conceive of an original, boundless ocean of all excellence and perfection, from which all limited perfections have been derived.

There is no evidence for more, based on any effects or appearances that *one original Cause* cannot account for. Indeed, all the appearances of connection, mutual dependencies of parts, and similarity of structure in those things which are very remote from each other, lead us to a unity of *design* and *power*. This sufficiently shows the futility of *Polytheism*, if anyone ever truly believed in a plurality of *original beings*. The wiser *Heathens* held a different kind of *Polytheism*; and that of the common people arose from low conceptions of the *Deities* as weak and imperfect, subject to distraction and confusion by a multitude of cares, or by a vast providence, and, like men, embarrassed when they undertake too much. One *almighty* and *omniscient Being* can preside easily over all, without toil or confusion.

<margin>Omnipresent.</margin>
The continual power exerted in all parts of the universe, and the unlimited nature of the *original Being*, lead us to conceive of him as possessing such *omnipresence* and *immensity* as is required for universal knowledge and action. And *that* which is *original* must be eternal.

<margin>Goodness is the source of creation.</margin>
What other motive to create could there be, but a desire to communicate perfection and happiness? *God* cannot be imagined as being primarily concerned with gaining glory from creatures who are infinitely below himself. And all desire for glory must assume that something is already recognized as excellent—that some quality of his nature, or some affection, is essentially the object of his approval. And what other quality can we suppose to be the object of his highest approval than perfect goodness, which always inclines him to share happiness? This inclination must move him to display his own excellencies to his rational creatures through his works, so that he may be the source of the highest happiness to them—the noblest object of their contemplation and reverence, of their love, esteem, hope, and secure confidence, and the best pattern for their imitation. *God* displays his perfections to make his creatures happy through the knowledge and love of them, and not to gain any new happiness for himself from their praises or admiration.

<margin>The holiness of the Deity.</margin>
The *wisdom* and *goodness* of God show us his moral purity or holiness. Because he is independent, almighty, and wise, he cannot be in need; he can have no private goals that oppose the universal good, nor does he have any base appetites or passions. These are the only motivations for moral evil that we can imagine. In *God*, none of these can exist; there is nothing contrary to

<margin>The justice of God.</margin>
His conduct toward his creatures must be such as goodness and wisdom suggest. His laws must be good and just, adapted to the interest and perfection of the whole. No unworthy favorites shall find in him a partial tenderness inconsistent with the general good or the sacred authority of his laws; no private views shall stop the execution of their sanctions, as long as the general interest and the maintenance of the majesty of these laws require it. It is no unjust partiality that the lot of some should have many advantages over that of others. As we showed above, the best order and harmony of the whole may require this. These are the natural notions of justice in a *moral governor*. It is a branch of goodness joined with wisdom, which must lead the *governor* to such conduct as may support the authority and influence of his laws for the general good.

<margin>What affections are suited to the Divine Perfections.</margin>
**I. IN** the consideration of the several enjoyments of our nature, we showed the frequent occasion men must have for recourse to Divine Providence for the security of their enjoyments and a stable tranquility of mind under the adversities of this life which may befall ourselves, or the objects of our tenderest affections. We established in the preceding chapter that grand foundation of our happiness: the existence and moral perfections of *God*, and his providence. <margin>This is known by the moral sense.</margin>

Indeed, it points them out as being of a more sacred obligation. <margin>Worship is internal or external.</margin>
The worship suited to the Divine Attributes is either internal or external: the former consists in the sentiments and affections of the soul; the latter in the natural expressions of them.

<margin>What is owed to the natural perfections.</margin>
Our duty in respect to the natural attributes of *God* is to entertain and cultivate, through frequent meditation, the highest admiration for that immensely great *original Being* from which all others are derived; and to restrain all low imaginations which might diminish our veneration; all conceptions of the *Deity* as limited, physical, resembling any animal or human form, or confined within certain places: all of which seem inconsistent with his infinite power and perfection, and his original, uncaused existence.

<margin>The affections owed to the moral perfections: love, esteem, and veneration.</margin>

Wisdom and power joined to it raise love, esteem, and admiration to the highest level. They must excite the most zealous study to please, the greatest caution against offending, and provide the highest satisfaction in the consciousness of conforming to the will of a Being possessed of such excellencies. <margin>Trust and resignation.</margin>
A firm belief in these divine perfections produces trust, resignation, and entire submission to everything ordered by Providence, from a strong conviction that everything is ordered for the best—for the greatest universal interest and for the interest of every good person. Vast goodness must desire the best state for the whole; omniscience must discover the means; and omnipotence can carry them out. Everything becomes acceptable in the place where God orders or permits it; not necessarily for its own sake, but through implicit trust or faith that it is necessary for the purposes of infinite goodness and wisdom. We know that the kind intentions of the Deity are to be carried out partly through the active virtues of good people, and that a great share of their supreme perfection and happiness consists in these virtues. Therefore, our dependence on Divine Power and Goodness will not hinder any of our kind or virtuous purposes, but rather invigorate and support us with joyful hopes of success. The same resignation and trust we exercise for ourselves and our own interests, we shall also exercise for everyone dear to us through virtuous bonds, and for every honorable cause in which we or others are involved—trusting that it will either prosper in this life or lead to the future glory and happiness of those who have supported it.

The external advantages we provide to each other by our active virtues, *God* could have immediately granted by his power without any action of ours; but, such was his goodness, he chose that we should enjoy some share of that divine and honorable pleasure of doing good to others; and, by the exercise of our kind affections and by our *moral faculty*, we do participate in it. The joys we feel in being honored by our fellows are also his gift to us, through his implanting this sense of moral excellence and that natural delight we perceive in the approval and esteem of others.

All the pleasures of knowledge, all the effects of art and invention, are owed to him, who *taught us more than the beasts of the field, and made us wiser than the birds of heaven*; to him we owe the fact that we can discern the beauty, kind intention, and wisdom of his works, and thus adore the traces of his wisdom and goodness; that we can discern moral beauty, the affections and conduct which are acceptable to him, and most resemble the *Divine Beauty*; that we can discover his perfections and imitate them; and that we can give secure tranquility to our souls through an entire confidence in them and resignation to his providence.
