Without this confidence in *God*, what can we call secure? Our bodies and all external things are obviously uncertain; so is the prosperity of our friends, and of all the objects of our generous affections. Their very virtues, though among the most stable things of life, are not secured against change. Some accidents can disturb their reason and their virtue. It is only the soul resigned to *God*, with firm trust in his perfections, that can promise to itself in the end everything happy and honorable.

In every good disposition, certain affections must arise upon their natural occasions, whether they can affect the state of the object or not. Although we were fully aware of our own impotence, or lack of opportunity to do good deeds or make returns, a disposition would be odious which had no love and esteem for great excellence, and no gratitude for great benefits. Thus joy must arise in a good heart upon the prosperity of one beloved, though we cannot add to it; and sorrow upon his adversity, though we cannot remove or alleviate it. The lack of such affections, where there are such strong natural causes presented, must suggest a depravity of soul which we cannot avoid abhorring upon reflection. <margin>The influence of religion on human society.</margin>
It is a needless inquiry to ask whether a society of *Atheists* could exist, or whether their condition would be better or worse than that of people possessed by some wicked superstition. True religion clearly increases the happiness of both individuals and societies. If you remove all religion, you remove some of the strongest bonds and some of the noblest motives for faithfulness and energy in all social duties. It is also plain that some systems of religious beliefs, even where much wicked superstition is included, may contain many noble principles, rules, and motives. These have positive effects on the minds of those who are not involved in carrying out the goals of the superstition. It is of no importance to determine whether such superstitions have worse effects than *Atheism*. They may, regarding people in certain positions, though they do not hurt the rest considerably. The experiment of a society of *Atheists* has never yet been conducted. Suppose we grant that the effects of some superstitions were worse than those of *Atheism*; this is actually a credit to religion. The best state of religion is incomparably happier than any condition of *Atheism*, and the corruption of the best things can be the most harmful. An excess of nourishing food may be more dangerous than an excess of food that is less nourishing; spoiled wines are more dangerous than bad water. It is the task of rational minds to embrace all the blessings of a true religion and guard against any corruption of it, without seeking to discover what motives for some types of virtue might remain under the joyless, wretched thought that the universe is under no providence, but left to chance or to a blind and undesigning necessity. If religion, when corrupted, causes great harm, then a pure and good religion is a powerful engine for much good.

<margin>*Mistakes.*</margin>
III. Many are discouraged from a vigorous cultivation of their minds for the reception of all virtues by a rash prejudice. They are fretted by such disappointments and quit the pursuits of virtue, desponding of any valuable enjoyment attending it.

## C H A P.  I.

->*The Circumstances which increase or diminish the* MORAL GOOD, *or* EVIL *of Actions.*<-

Having shown, in the former book, that the course of life which GOD and NATURE recommend to us as most lovely and most conducive to the agent's true happiness, is that which is intended for the general good of mankind in the wisest manner that our reason and observation can suggest; we proceed, in this book, to inquire more particularly into the proper means of promoting the happiness of mankind by our actions, which is the same thing as inquiring into the more specific laws of nature. <header>CIRCUMSTANCES affecting</header>

## BOOK II.
<image-desc>horizontal decorative flourish</image-desc>

<margin>The basis for imputation: that actions flow from and reveal the affections.</margin>
I. The basis for all imputation* of actions as virtuous or vicious is, "that they flow from some affection in the agent, and thus are evidence of his character and affections." Virtue, as it was proved in the previous book, consists primarily in the affections. The highest kind of it is the calm and fixed principle of goodwill toward the greatest system; and love, esteem, gratitude, and resignation to *God*, based on a full conviction of his moral perfections, and a constant, prevailing desire to make even further progress toward that moral perfection of which we perceive ourselves to be capable. The lower kinds are those specific benevolent affections and passions pursuing the good of particular societies, or individuals, consistent with the general good. This, one would think, could hardly be a matter of debate among Christians, after the summary of the law delivered to us, † namely, *Loving God and our neighbor*. If virtue is not placed in the affections, but in some other faculty different from the will, such as *reason* or *intellect*, then love would have to be called an act of the understanding, which is contrary to all language.

<margin>Qualities and circumstances necessary for the morality of actions.</margin>
II. From this description it is easy to determine what circumstances affect the morality of actions or omissions, increasing or diminishing the moral good or evil in them; or making actions good, which otherwise would have been evil; or evil, which otherwise would have been good.

<margin>Liberty.</margin>
First. It is manifest that whatever action, or rather event, happened not as a consequence of one’s will, ei-

<page-num>229</page-num>
<header>the MORALITY of ACTIONS.</header>

<margin>
CHAP. I.
</margin>
[ei]ther at present, or in some prior time, cannot be attributed as either good or evil. Nor can any omission or abstaining from action be attributed as good or evil to someone who could not have performed it through any efforts and was aware of this impossibility. Such events or omissions can provide no evidence of an affection, whether good or bad. Events, however, are only called *necessary* in relation to an agent if he could not prevent them even though he seriously desired to; they are not "necessary" simply because he cannot help desiring them due to his strong aversions or habits. Only those things are called *impossible* which no efforts of his can accomplish by *any* means. We call anything possible which a person who heartily desires it can accomplish, whether by his own power or by any help from others that he can obtain.*

<margin>
Necessary events are not moral.
</margin>
These alone are the necessary and completely unimputable events † which no present desire or action of ours can prevent, nor could they have been prevented by any previous diligence or care that we should have exercised regarding such matters. Such events that previous forethought and care could have prevented—even though they are now unavoidable—are in some measure voluntary ‡ and imputable, whether they happen from free agency or from natural, inanimate causes. Thus, if a person, through negligence in his office, allows banks or mounds to decay, he cannot prevent the flood when a storm comes; and yet it is justly considered voluntary and imputable to him.

---

<note>\* This explains the common maxim: "There is no attribution of things that are impossible or necessary."</note>
<note>† Involuntary both in themselves and in their cause.</note>
<note>‡ Voluntary in themselves, but not in their cause.</note>

<summary>This page defines the limits of moral responsibility, explaining that individuals cannot be blamed or praised for necessary or impossible events they cannot control. However, it notes that events are still considered voluntary and imputable if they resulted from a past failure of care or negligence.</summary>

Thus, the failure to perform actions that are now impossible is justly attributed to a person when those actions might have been possible had that previous diligence been used which is expected of a good person. A lazy, extravagant man cannot now pay his debts; yet, because a prior course of prudent economy would have prevented this injury to his creditors, the non-payment is still attributable to him. In these cases, indeed, the unavoidable event or omission—which is contrary to his current strong desire—shows no current evil motivation. But the former negligence, which made him incapable of doing justice, indicates a prior blameworthy defect in his character. And it is here that the guilt properly lies. Two people may be equally criminal in the sight of God and their own consciences even when the outcomes of their conduct are very different. Suppose there is equal negligence in both, and that both become insolvent, but one, through an unexpected inheritance, pays his debts; the other, though equally willing, remains incapable of it. They are equally criminal, even though one, by accident, does no wrong in the end to his creditors.

<margin>What conscience is.</margin>
V. The questions about vincible ignorance, and consciences that are erroneous or doubtful, are only difficult because of the ambiguity of words. Conscience sometimes signifies the *moral faculty* itself: sometimes "the judgment of the understanding concerning the motives and effects of actions, upon which the *moral sense* approves or condemns them." And when we have established certain maxims and rules concerning conduct which is virtuous or vicious, and conceive them to be—as they truly are—the laws given to us by *God*, the author of nature and of all our powers; or when we are persuaded that other divine laws are revealed to us in a different manner, then conscience may be defined as "Our judgment concerning actions compared with the *law*."

Aristotle* well observes that “many points in *morals*, when applied to individual cases, cannot be exactly determined; but good men know them by a sort of sensation: the good, experienced man is thus the final measure of all things.” This holds true in general: “the greater the diligence and caution regarding our duty is, the better the character is; and the less the diligence and caution is, the worse the character is, when other circumstances are equal.”

## General Rules for judging the MORALITY of ACTIONS, based on the Affections that excite or oppose them.

ALTHOUGH people cannot accurately judge the degrees of virtue or vice in the actions of others, because their internal motives are unknown, certain general rules can be completely certain and useful for judging ourselves. We have no great need to apply these rules to others, as doing so must be extremely uncertain.

<margin>General rules about the importance of actions.</margin>
1. Where kind affections alone are the motives of action, the good achieved by any person is equal to the strength of these affections and his ability combined. The strength of affection, therefore, is directly proportional to the good achieved and inversely proportional to his abilities; or, in simpler terms, when the good done by two people is equal while their abilities are unequal, the person whose abilities were smaller shows the better heart.

<margin>How considerations of private interest affect the morality of actions.</margin>
2. Where people are also motivated by considerations of private interest, the effect of these selfish desires is to be subtracted, and the remainder shows the effect of the virtuous disposition. Where motives of private interest discouraged someone from a good action that was performed anyway, the virtue appears higher by overcoming these motives.

3. In the same way, we calculate the moral turpitude of unkind or basely selfish affections leading us to cause injury. The strength of these affections is directly proportional to the evil achieved and inversely proportional to the person's abilities. That is, where

The author argues that while we cannot perfectly judge others' internal motives, these principles are essential for self-evaluation.</summary>

If two actions were equal, the one that flowed from a calm, settled principle of kindness is more approved than another resulting from some turbulent passion. The superior excellence of these calm dispositions is universally acknowledged; it shows men what temperament nature recommends for their cultivation, through all the power we have over our affections. Here we also see the reason why no great virtue is perceived in our kindness toward our offspring, relatives, or even benefactors. Strong, specific passions naturally arise toward people so related to us, whether we have any of the more extensive affections active in our hearts or not; and few characters are so depraved as to be void of these natural affections. Indeed, the lack of them—for reasons soon to be mentioned—would suggest a temperament depraved to a most hateful degree.

The following maxims seem quite probable, or certain:

<margin>Several general rules.</margin>
1. That affections of equal degrees of extent or strength are not expected from persons in unequal circumstances and opportunities, even if they originally had equal temperaments. More is demanded from those who have had instruction, leisure for meditation, and access to better positions.

2. Such services as are useful to others, and involve no expense or labor for the agent, are justly expected from everyone toward all who need them. They are but slight evidence of virtue, but refusing them is very hateful and shows a temperament devoid of humanity.

3. Furthermore, we universally condemn the refusal of such smaller expenses or troubles that can hardly disturb the happiness of one’s life, when it is necessary for any important advantage even to a stranger.

4. The greater the expense or trouble one submits to for the benefit of others, the greater evidence of his virtue it must be to others.

<margin>How narrower affections should yield to more extensive ones.</margin> The same difficulties may appear in determining precisely how far narrower affections in particular cases should yield to more extensive ones; or how far the interests of families, kindred, benefactors, friends, our party, or country, should be sacrificed to more extensive interests to avoid a bad character or the charge of guilt. A calm mind, concerned about its own conduct, will blame every defect of that most perfect moral order which requires sacrificing all narrower interests to more extensive ones. But there is something so beautiful and so engaging in many narrower affections of the soul that we judge less rigidly the conduct of men who, from such lovely principles, neglect the highest perfection. And as only a small degree of attention and discernment can be reasonably expected from men of lower stations and capacities, who are much encumbered by procuring the necessities of life for themselves and their immediate dependents, nature is far from leading us to pronounce a character bad which does not in all cases adhere to the most exact rules of perfection. But nevertheless, the attentive, reflecting mind cannot help but see the fairest mark set up by *God* in his heart: a clear idea of perfection. The nearer he can come to it, the better and more excellent he is. Nor was it the Divine intention that we should satisfy ourselves by merely avoiding such

conduct that is a matter of infamy. Two general maxims are abundantly obvious in these cases.

1. First, to maintain a calm and most extensive affection toward universal happiness as the strongest principle of the soul—able to control all narrower affections whenever there is any opposition—and to sacrifice all narrower interests to the most extensive, while still preserving every tender affection in the various relations of life with as much strength as a just subordination to the superior will allows, is the highest perfection of human virtue.

2. And yet, when some of these narrower, kind affections exceed their proper proportion and overcome the more extensive ones, the moral deformity is alleviated in proportion to the moral beauty of that narrower affection by which the more extensive one is overpowered. Thus, it is more excusable if we do something hurtful to the general interest out of zeal for our country or for a whole people, than if the same thing had been done to aggrandize a party, a cabal, or a family. And any of those tender affections lessen the guilt more than any merely selfish principle—such as greed, ambition, or sensuality—could have done.

These are regarded as innocent actions, or even as matters of duty. And even where the resulting public harm is greater than the harm we escape through the action, the guilt, though not completely removed, is greatly lessened. Still, such actions are moral and attributable as morally good or evil.

## CHAP. III.

### The general Notions of RIGHTS, and LAWS, explained; with their Divisions.

<margin>Right and wrong in action.</margin>
I. FROM the constitution of our *moral faculty* explained above, we have our notions of *right* and *wrong* as characteristics of affections and actions. The affections approved as right are either universal goodwill and the love of moral excellence, or such particular kind affections as are consistent with these. The actions approved as *right* are those wisely intended either for the general good, or for such good of some particular society or individual as is consistent with it. The contrary affections and actions are *wrong*.

<margin>Goodness material, and formal.</margin>
An action is called *materially good* when in fact it tends to the interest of the system, as far as we can judge of its tendency; or to the good of some part consistent with that of the system, whatever the affections of the agent were. An action is *formally good* when it flows from good affections in a just proportion. A good man deliberating † which of several actions proposed he shall choose, regards and compares the *material goodness* of them, and then is determined by his moral sense, which invariably prefers that which appears most conducive to the happiness and virtue of mankind. But in judging of his ‡ past actions he con-

<note>† Antecedent conscience (<term>Conscientia antecedens</term>).</note>
<note>‡ Subsequent conscience (<term>Conscientia subsequens</term>).</note>

<margin>The notion of rights;</margin>
Our notion of *right* as a moral quality belonging to some person, as when we say one has a *right* to such things, is a much more complex conception. Whatever action we would deem either as virtuous or innocent were it done by the agent in certain circumstances, we say he has a *right* to do it. Whatever one so possesses and enjoys in certain circumstances, that we would deem it a wrong action in any other to disturb or interrupt his possession, we say *it is his right*, or he has a *right* to enjoy and possess it. Whatever demand one has upon another in such circumstances that we would deem it wrong conduct in that other not to comply with it, we say one has a *right* to what is thus demanded. Or we may say more briefly, a man has a *right* to do, possess, or demand anything, † "when his acting, possessing, or obtaining from another in these circumstances tends to the good of society, or to the interest of the individual consistently with the rights of others and the general good of society, and obstructing him would have the contrary tendency."

Our *moral sense* also has other immediate objects of approval—many narrower affections—which we must immediately approve without thinking of their tendency toward the interest of a system. In the same way, we immediately condemn many unkind passions and actions without considering their distant effects on society. When someone, through innocent industry and kind affections, procures for himself and those he loves the means of ease and pleasure, every good spectator is pleased that he should enjoy them; the spectator must immediately condemn the disturbance of his possession and enjoyment without thinking of the effects of such injustice on a community. Indeed, if any grand interest of a community requires that he be deprived of some part of his acquisitions, then we see a superior moral form: a public interest, which a good mind must regard more. A more extensive affection, appearing more lovely than the narrower one, justifies the mind in controlling the narrower. The former approval was equally immediate, but this latter is of a higher kind, to which the former is naturally * subordinate.

<margin>
*Perfect and imperfect rights;*
</margin>
III. Rights are divided into perfect and imperfect, depending on whether they are more or less necessary to be maintained and observed in society. Every legitimate right contributes in some way to the public interest and is founded upon such a tendency. Observing and fulfilling every legitimate right of others is a matter of conscience, necessary to obtain the approval of God and our own hearts. But some rights are of such a nature that the interest of society requires they should always be maintained and fulfilled for everyone who possesses them, even through methods of force where gentler measures prove ineffective; these are called *perfect rights*. These include the rights every innocent person has to his life; to a good reputation; to the integrity and health of his body; to the gains of his honest industry; and to act according to his own choice within the limits of the law of nature. This right we call natural liberty, of which liberty of conscience is not only an essential but an unalienable branch. These rights should be maintained for all people, unless a more general interest of mankind requires any limitation of them. Society cannot survive unless these rights are

Other rights, though just as truly sacred in the sight of *God* and our own consciences, are yet of such a nature that, for certain remote reasons of public utility, they must not be asserted by violence or compulsion, but left to the goodness of other men’s hearts. These are the *imperfect rights*. Respecting and fulfilling them for everyone who possesses them is of great advantage and an ornament to human life; and violating or refusing to fulfill them to others may, in many cases, be as criminal in the sight of *God* as the violation of perfect rights. However, because they are not of such absolute necessity for the survival of society among men, and because there are the most obvious reasons why they should be left to men’s honor and conscience, they are not a matter of compulsion. Such are the rights of the poor to relief from the wealthy; the rights of all men to kindnesses that cause no trouble or expense; the rights of friends and benefactors to friendly and grateful returns; and the right of every good man to such services as are of much greater importance to him than any small trouble or loss they cause to men in high positions or fortunes.

<margin>What rights may be opposite.</margin>
Now, as no action, enjoyment, or demand—and its contrary—can be equally useful to society, nature has in no instance established proper rights that are opposite to one another. Imperfect rights of humanity may be opposite to external rights; but as neither the former nor the latter entitles one to use force with a good conscience, war can never be truly just on both sides. Any obligation in conscience to comply with the external shadows of right which others may have can arise only from prudence regarding our own interest, or from some remote concerns about the harm that may, in some cases, result to society from opposing them—and not from any sense of duty toward the person who insists on them in opposition to humanity.

<margin>
*The degrees from imperfect to perfect are innumerable.*
</margin>

V. By dividing rights into the two classes of perfect and imperfect, we do not suggest that all those of either class are of the same importance or necessity; that the guilt of violating all perfect rights is equal; or that violating all imperfect rights is equally criminal. There is plainly a gradation from the weakest claim of humanity to the highest perfect right, by innumerable steps. Every worthy man, though not in distress, has a claim upon the great and opulent for any good office in their way for improving his condition, when no one of greater merit, or greater indigence, has an interfering claim. This is among the lowest imperfect rights or claims. A good man in distress has a higher claim. One who has done eminent public services has a higher still: one who had done singular services of an honorable kind to men now in power has a stronger claim upon them, especially if he has fallen into distress. All these we call imperfect rights. The greater the merit and natural causes of love there are in the person who has these claims, the nearer also they approach to perfect rights. A worthy man in distress has an imperfect claim to the necessities of life upon all who can relieve him, but on his children his claim is almost perfect, not only for a bare support, but for such conveniences of life suited to the parent's station as they can afford without distressing themselves. The sense of an honest man, practiced in the affairs of life,

<margin>
CHAP. 3.
***
What their strength depends upon.
</margin>
In general, rights are more sacred the greater their importance is to the public good, the greater the evils are that follow from violating them, the less the trouble or expense is of observing them, and the greater the merit or causes of love are in the persons who possess them. And the stronger the claim is, the greater is the crime of opposing it; and the smaller the degree of virtue is in complying with it.

On the other hand, the less the detriment is that follows from violating a right, the greater the trouble or expense is of fulfilling or complying with it, and the smaller the merit of the person is, the weaker the right is; but then, more virtue is evidenced by respecting it, provided there is a proportionally higher regard for the higher claims of others; and the moral turpitude of neglecting it is that much less. Small virtue is shown by paying a just debt, by abstaining from outrages and violence, by common returns of good deeds where we have been highly obliged, or by common duty to a worthy parent in distress; but conduct contrary to such sacred claims would be most detestable. Acts of singular generosity to a worthy man who has no special claim upon us are greater evidence of a good character (if we show a proportionally higher passion for goodness where there is equal merit and peculiar claims upon us) than acts that are equally beneficent toward a relative or a great benefactor.

<summary>This page discusses the factors that determine the strength and sacredness of different rights, noting that violating a strong right is a great crime while fulfilling a weak right demonstrates greater virtue.</summary>

<margin>Right and obligation are relative.</margin>
VI. To every right there corresponds an *obligation*, perfect or imperfect, just as the right is. The term obligation is both complex and ambiguous. We primarily say one is obliged to an action “when he must find, from the constitution of human nature, that he and every attentive observer must disapprove of its omission as morally evil.” The word is sometimes taken to mean “a strong motive of interest established by the will of some powerful *superior* to engage us to act as he requires.” In the former sense, obligation is founded on our moral faculty; in the latter, it seems to set it aside. But in describing the *superior* who can establish obligation, we include not only sufficient force or power, but also a just right to govern; and this justice or right will lead us back again to our *moral faculty*. Because of this ambiguity †, brilliant men have sharply contradicted each other; some asserting an obligation that exists prior to all considerations of interest or laws, while others derive the original source of all obligation from the law or will of an omnipotent Being. This leads us to consider the general doctrine of laws and the foundation of the right of governing rational agents, to which corresponds their obligation to obey.

<margin>The right of the Deity to govern all.</margin>

<margin>Human power not thus founded.</margin>

Some extraordinary cases may be excepted.

<margin>Laws natural and positive in two senses.</margin>
IX. Laws are divided into *natural* and *positive*. However, these two terms are used with very different meanings. Sometimes the division is based on the *different manners of promulgation*; and then by *natural laws* are understood the moral determinations of the heart and the conclusions of right reason drawn from these determinations and other observations of nature; and by *positive laws*, such as are promulgated in words or writing, whatever the subject matter of them may be.

<margin>Laws necessary or not necessary.</margin>
Others take the division expressed by these words from the diversity of the *matter of laws*; as some laws declare the natural, direct, and necessary means of supporting the dignity of human nature and promoting the public good; so that either opposite or different laws could not be equally useful—indeed, they would be harmful to society. These they call *natural*: such are all the laws of justice and humanity. Other laws have indeed in their intention some good end, and with a view to it require certain means, but these are not always the sole, or the necessary, or even the preferable means. The same good end may be obtained by different means, and these equally convenient or effective, and yet it may be necessary for the good of a society that a certain set of means be agreed upon for all. Furthermore, certain institutions make some practices useful which in their own nature were of no use. Thus, some rites

<margin>*The wise ends of positive laws.*</margin>
The most frequent occasions for positive laws are those where the same good ends may be obtained in different ways, but it is necessary that some one way be fixed for everyone in a certain district. Thus, social worship can neither be performed, nor courts of justice be held, unless times and places are determined; and yet it is seldom found that any one time is more suitable than another for any natural reason. In like manner, in the administration of justice, there are different forms of process, different penalties for crimes, and different times for executions. It is convenient that all these points should be known and settled for a whole society; and yet no one of the possible determinations can be said to be absolutely best, such that the smallest variation would make it worse.

<margin>*Positive laws are not useless or arbitrary.*</margin>
Positive laws are quite different from what we call arbitrary or imperious laws, such as those enacted merely from a display of power, without being subservient to the public interest.

To the obligation of a law, promulgation is necessary; not that every subject must actually know it, but that everyone has it in his power, through such diligence as he is capable of, to attain knowledge of it. The penalties of laws may be justly exacted where the laws have not been actually known, when

<margin>How the law of nature is perfect.</margin>
**X.** As the laws of nature include not merely the original moral determinations of the mind, but likewise the practical conclusions made by the reasoning and reflection of men upon the constitution of nature—showing what conduct is worthy and tends toward the public good—there needs to be little controversy about their perfection, as all must admit that the reason even of the most ingenious and most improved people is still imperfect. And it may be very possible that a superior being could see that a certain rule of conduct is conducive to the public good, which no human could ever have discovered to be useful. As for the bulk of mankind, they may indeed easily discover the general and most necessary rules, but they seldom can find out or even understand well the reasons upon which some of the more specific laws—which nevertheless have a substantial foundation in nature—are built. If by the "system of the laws of nature" one means the very constitution of nature itself, or the objective evidence laid before rational beings as a whole, this is no doubt perfect; but its perfection does not supersede the usefulness of the revelation of laws

<margin>Its imperfection is no blemish on providence.</margin>
We should not criticize providence on account of this imperfection, for reasons * mentioned above, any more than we criticize it for our small bodily strength, or the shortness of our lives. If we use our powers and opportunities well, the condition of human life in this world will be, in the main, an agreeable and happy state; and yet by divine revelation, or even by accurate reasonings of wise men, much may be discovered for the improvement of this life; and many fine institutions may be contrived, the reasons for which neither anyone in the ruder nations, nor the populace in the more civilized, shall ever apprehend.

<margin>All laws should aim at some good.</margin>
But this holds in general: that all wise and just laws have some tendency toward the general happiness, or toward the good of some part of the system subservient to and consistent with the general good. The moral good in obedience consists in either a direct intention of this good end proposed by the law, whether we know it fully ourselves or implicitly trust to the goodness of the legislator; or in some grateful affection toward the legislator. Where obedience flows only from fear of punishment, or hope of reward, it has no moral excellence, though in some cases it may be innocent.

<margin>How the law of nature is immutable.</margin>
XI. Precepts of the law of nature, or these practical observations, are considered immutable and eternal because some rules—or rather the dispositions which gave origin to them and in which they are founded—must always tend to the general good, and the contrary to the general detriment, in such a system of creatures as we are. But we must not imagine that all the special precepts of the law of nature are immutable in the way they are commonly stated universally. If we make the precepts immutable, we must allow many exceptions as parts of the precept, or understand the precept as holding only generally in ordinary cases. Since the precept is indeed no more than a conclusion from observing what sort of conduct is ordinarily useful to society, some unique cases may happen in which departing from the ordinary rule may be more for the general interest than following it. And some wise human institutions may take away or limit some rights which were formerly sacredly confirmed to each individual by the law of nature. Before civil government, each person had a right through private violence, when gentler methods were ineffective, to obtain reparation for a wrong from its author. But in civil government, private individuals no longer have a right to use those means. In the same way, civil laws justly limit our use of our own property and take some share of it for public exigencies, whereas prior to some political institution, the general law of nature allowed each person the full use of all their own acquisitions and the right of disposing of them at

It specifically notes that individuals relinquish certain natural rights, like the private use of force or absolute property control, when they enter into a political society.</summary>

pleasure. Unique cases of necessity are also justly deemed exceptions to ordinary laws. It is normally harmful to use the property of another without his consent; but an innocent man, when he cannot otherwise save his life while fleeing from an unjust enemy, does no wrong by taking the horse of another when he cannot wait for the owner's consent.

The two fundamental precepts of "loving God and promoting universal happiness" admit no exceptions; indeed, in the latter precept are founded all the exceptions to the special laws of nature: all the rights of departing from ordinary rules in cases of unique necessity, and all the limitations of our rights by any wise institutions. All these are justified by their tendency in certain cases, and upon certain suppositions, to produce a greater good for the system than would result from following the ordinary rule.

A debtor is bound by the law to make payment: but a remission or release from the creditor frees him from this obligation. We should not, therefore, say that every creditor has a power of dispensing with the laws of nature. The more perceptive Schoolmen, based on these considerations, do not allow the extraordinary commands given to *Moses* and *Joshua* to be considered dispensations from the laws of nature. But it is needless to debate about words. If the law itself is wise and just in the full extent in which it is expressed, no act of any superior can make counteracting it innocent or virtuous. But most of the specific laws of nature cannot be expressed in strictly universal words without including exceptions for many cases, particularly those involving God exercising his rightful dominion.

<margin>*What is commonly meant by them.*</margin>
Dispensations, therefore, according to the full intention of the *Canonists*, are only to be granted regarding laws that are either capricious or imprudent, or too universally expressed without mentioning the reasonable and just exceptions that should have been included in the laws themselves. In the laws of nature, there can be no place for them, since the same reason and observation that discover the ordinary general rule also discover all the exceptions, which are therefore parts of the law.

<margin>What a moral state is.</margin>
WHEN we speak of the different states of men, by a *state* we do not mean any temporary condition a man may be in for a short time, nor any obligation he may be under regarding one or two temporary acts, but "a permanent condition including a long series of rights and obligations." The conditions men may be in regarding sickness or health, beauty or deformity, or any other circumstances which are considered in other arts, are irrelevant to our purpose. The moral states of men always include a series of moral obligations and rights.

<margin>*The state of liberty always exists.*</margin>
II. This state of natural liberty exists among those who have no common superior or magistrate, and are only subject to *God* and the law of nature. It is no fictitious state; it has always existed and must exist among men, unless the whole earth should become one empire. The parental power of the first parents of mankind must soon have expired when their children reached maturity (as we shall show hereafter), or at least when the parents died. This state of liberty probably continued for a long time among the several heads of families before civil governments were established. And it is not improbable that it still exists in some more primitive parts of the world. Indeed, it must still exist among the various independent states in relation to each other, and among the subjects of different states who may happen to meet on the ocean or in lands where no civil power is established. The laws of nature are the laws of this state, whether they are confirmed by civil power or not; and it is the main purpose of civil laws and their sanctions to restrain men more effectively from violating them through visible punishments. <margin>Rights belong to individuals, societies, or all of humanity.</margin>

As it is said that men “have rights to do, possess, or demand from others whatever the happiness of the individual requires and the public interest of humanity permits them to be allowed to do, possess, or obtain from others;” and as all rights and obligations are founded on some tendency toward either general happiness or the happiness of individuals consistent with the general good (which must result from the happiness of individuals), rights may be divided into those of individuals, those of particular societies or corporations, and those belonging generally to all of humanity as a system. This division depends on the subject or persons in whom these rights reside or to whom they belong, and for whose benefit they are directly established. The first type are established directly for the benefit of individuals by the law of nature; the second for the common interest of a corporation or state, although no more directly for any one member than another; in the third type of rights, no single individual or corporation may be more concerned than another, and yet it may be in the general interest of humanity that such rights be asserted and maintained. Each of these three classes may be either *perfect* or *imperfect*, depending on whether they are more or less necessary to be maintained for the public interest, and whether they are of such a nature as to allow for compulsion and force in their defense or pursuit; or, on the other hand, whether they must be left to each...

How private rights are known.

IV. The private rights of individuals are clearly suggested to us in the constitution of our nature by these two circumstances together: first, natural desires and senses pointing out the gratifications we are suited to receive as parts of that happiness the author of our nature has intended for us; and secondly, by the powers of reason and reflection which can discover how far the gratification of our natural desires is consistent with the finer principles in our constitution, which, as we showed above, are destined to govern and control all our particular desires. These principles show the limits to be placed not only on selfish desires aiming at the private happiness of the agent, but on the several narrower generous affections and the gratifications which they pursue; and they plainly reveal that the grand end of our being is indeed the promotion of the most universal happiness, but that our heart at the same time may approve our conduct not only in acts of specific beneficence toward persons especially dear to us in some of the closer relations, provided this beneficence does not interfere with more extensive interests; but also in the pursuit of all private gratifications which are consistent with these interests and do not engross the mind or shrink it too much within itself.

This fragile and uncertain condition of our outward happiness must powerfully move us to cultivate peace and goodwill in society, and to avoid all offense and provocation of others; since we risk more by incurring the hatred of others than we can probably hope to gain. Though the strength of men is unequal, skill can supply the deficiencies of strength; and a stubborn resolution can supply the deficiencies of both, so as to deprive an adversary of life and all his other enjoyments, as well as the advantage he aimed for by his provocative injury. Thus, when men are not forced into violence for their own defense, peace and justice are still desirable to the powerful and the clever as well as to others; since they do not know what universal indignation may be raised by anything injurious—arising from the *moral sense* of mankind, from sympathy with the sufferer, and from fears of their own future dangers. A friendly, just, and kind conduct, as it naturally attracts the goodwill, esteem, and helpfulness of others, is the only likely method of obtaining security and all the external advantages and pleasures of life.

## C H A P. V.

### *The Private* RIGHTS *of* MEN; *first such as are called* NATURAL; *and the natural Equality of Men.*

<margin>Rights natural and adventitious.</margin>
I. **P**rivate rights of individuals, according to their different origins, are either *natural* or *adventitious*. The *natural* are those which each person has from the constitution of nature itself, without the intervention of any human invention, institution, agreement, or deed. The *adventitious* arise from some human institution, agreement, or action.

<margin>The natural rights to life, and safety.</margin>
The following natural rights of each individual seem to be of the perfect sort. 1. A right to life, and to that physical health which nature has given, belongs to every person as a human being, as long as no important public interest requires him to be exposed to death or wounds. This right is violated by unjust assaults, maiming, or murdering. The innate desire for life and self-preservation suggests this right to everyone, as does also our immediate sense of moral evil in all cruelty that causes unnecessary pain or a reduction of happiness to any of our fellows; not to mention the dismal expression on the human face caused by grievous pain or death, the sight of which must move every human heart with pity and terror, and an abhorrence of the intentional cause of such unnecessary suffering.

2. As nature has implanted in each man a desire for his own happiness, and many tender affections to—

<margin>A right to use what is common.</margin>
5. Each person has a natural right to the use of such things as are in their nature suited for the common use of all (of which more will be said hereafter); and has a similar right, by any innocent means, to acquire property in such goods as are fit for occupation and ownership, and have not been occupied by others. The natural desires of mankind, both of the selfish and social kind, show this right. And it is plainly cruel and unjust to hinder any innocent acquisitions of another: indeed, when some acquisitions would endanger the liberty, independence, or safety of his neighbors, they have a right either to prevent such acquisitions, or to oblige him who makes them to give sufficient security for the safety of others.

<margin>Right to society with others.</margin>
6. For similar reasons, every innocent person has a natural right to enter into an exchange of innocent services or commerce with all who are inclined to deal with him. It is injurious for any third person to interfere, or restrict his or their choice, when he has not acquired some right to direct their actions.

<margin>To the character of innocence.</margin>
7. As we all have a strong natural desire for esteem, and the greatest aversion to infamy, every man has a natural right to a simple character of integrity and honesty, and to dispositions fit for a social life, until he has forfeited this right by contrary conduct.

<margin>Natural equality of men.</margin>

These laws prohibit the greatest or wisest of mankind from inflicting any misery on the humblest, or depriving them of any of their natural rights or innocent acquisitions, when no public interest requires it. <margin>No one is naturally a slave.</margin>

<margin>Aristotle's doctrine considered.</margin>
III. This is intended against the doctrine of Aristotle and some others of the ancients: "that some men are naturally slaves, of low genius but great bodily strength for labor; and others are by nature masters of finer and wiser spirits, but weaker bodies; that the former are by nature destined to be subject to the latter, just as beasts of burden are subjected to men. That the inhabitants of certain countries, particularly Greece, are universally of finer spirits and destined to command, and that the rest of the world are fitted for slavery. That by this subordination of the more stupid and imprudent to the wise and ingenious, the universal interest of the system is best promoted, as that of the animal system is promoted by the power of the rational species over the irrational."

The power of education is surprising! This author, in these justly admired books of politics, is a zealous asserter of liberty and has seen the finest and most humane reasons for all the more equitable plans of civil power. <margin>*The importance of generosity.*</margin>
V. In generosity and benevolence, the importance of any gift to the recipient is proportional to both the value of the gift and his poverty; and the real loss to the giver is proportional to the said value, and inversely to his wealth: that is, the greater his wealth is, the less an honest heart will feel the loss of what it gives; and that sense of loss which a poor, greedy person may have over a trifle is not to be regarded. The virtue of any donation is, in the same manner, measured directly by the value of the gift, and inversely by the wealth of the giver, as far as people can judge by outward evidence; for in this way, the strength of a generous affection over a selfish one is clearly displayed.

The increase made to the happiness of the poor may be incomparably greater than the decrease in the happiness of the donor, when the donor is wealthy; and this shows that people in such circumstances are primarily obligated to be generous. <margin>Necessary cautions.</margin>
Several prudent cautions and general rules are provided regarding liberality. First, that it not be harmful to the morals of the recipient under a false appearance of advantage by encouraging them in laziness, meanness of character, or any vicious dispositions. And again, that it not be so immoderate as to exhaust its own source and prevent similar acts in the future when more worthy recipients may appear, or disqualify the donor from other duties of life toward those whom he may be more sacredly obliged to support.

<margin>Who to be preferred.</margin>

Thus, courtesy and hospitality to strangers, along with a general civility and helpfulness in behavior even toward unknown persons, are rightly considered strong evidence of a kind disposition; they are all the more lovely because they are not suspected of being motivated by self-interest.

<margin>BOOK II.</margin>
A truly great mind does good to others as its natural work, arising from its own sweet disposition and natural impulse to exercise those virtues, regardless of what returns are made. It achieves its main purpose when it performs its role well. But the lesser virtues of others are discouraged by ingratitude; and the ungrateful are the common enemies of all the needy, as they discourage generosity and, as far as they can, dry up the fountain from which the needy are to be supplied.

No precise measures can be fixed for returns of gratitude, any more than for generosity. Returning an exact equivalent to the benefits received would in many cases be too much, and in many too little. A kind, grateful heart, combined with common prudence, is its own true measure, *as the generous mind must devise generous things*. There is the same reason against having precise laws in this case as there is in the case of generosity.

There is a general obligation of gratitude upon us all toward those who have performed any generous or useful services to any valuable part of mankind: that we should esteem and honor them, promote their interests, and give them just praise—a sweet reward for noble minds—while protecting their characters against envy and detraction. Such conduct encourages every generous disposition and inspires men to imitate those who are eminently virtuous. The hope of honor outweighs those disadvantages and losses which often deter men of lesser virtue from any generous designs.

### C H A P. VI.
## The adventitious RIGHTS, REAL *and* PERSONAL, PROPERTY *or* DOMINION.

I. Adventitious rights are next to be considered,
<margin>*Real and personal rights.*</margin>
and they are either real, "when the right is directed toward some specific goods;" or *personal*, when "the right is directed toward a person, without any more specific claim upon one part of his goods than another." In personal rights, our claim is to some <term>prestation</term> (a performance of service or duty), or some value, leaving it to the person obligated to provide this value out of any part of his goods he pleases.

Among real rights, the primary one is property established in those things which are of some use in life. As to its origin, we first inquire into the general right which humankind has to the use of inanimate things and the lower animals; and then into that property which one person may have in certain things to the exclusion of others from all use of them.

When they attained the knowledge of a wise and good God, the creator of all these remarkable forms, and

These considerations would clearly show that a great increase of happiness and a reduction of misery for the whole must result from animals using the inanimate fruits of the earth for their support; and that consequently, it is right that they should use them, and that this is the intention of their Creator.

<margin>The right to the labor of beasts.</margin>

<margin>Animals may have rights.</margin>
And yet animals may very justly be said to have a right that no useless pain or misery should be inflicted on them. Men have indications of this right, and of their own corresponding obligation, by their sense of pity. It is plainly inhuman and immoral to cause animals any useless torment, or to deprive them of any such natural enjoyments that do not interfere with the interests of men. It is true animals have no concept of rights or of moral qualities; but infants are in the same situation, and yet they have their rights, which adults are obligated to maintain. Not to mention that frequent cruelty to animals may produce such a bad habit of mind that it may break out in similar treatment of our fellow humans.

Nature here points out another use; as we see many animal species led by their instincts to feed upon the flesh of other animals. The earth and animals must have had quite different constitutions; otherwise, these seeming evils could not have been prevented. The superior orders must have had some food provided: it is better that this food be alive for some time, and have some low sense and enjoyment, than be wholly unfeeling and only serve to nourish animals. It would be in the interest of an animal system that the nobler kinds should be increased, even if it diminished the numbers of the lower. A violent death at the hands of men may be a much lesser evil to the brutes than what they must otherwise have endured—and much earlier, too—had they been excluded from human care. Thus, the intention of nature to subject brute animals to men for food is abundantly manifest, and its tendency toward the general good of the system shows that men have a right to make this use of them.

If all these reasonings did not soon occur to men, it is probable they did not soon have any need for the flesh of animals. When they needed it, their own discernment might discover their right. V. We next consider the right of private property which one man may have to the exclusion of his fellow men.

<margin>The right of property.</margin>

And here first, the natural appetites and desires of men lead each person to take such things as are fit for present use, and yet lie in common, with a full persuasion of his right, if he has attained moral notions; as he sees that such things are destined for the use of men, and none of his fellows have obtained any prior right to them to preclude him from using them. He must also easily see that if another were to take from him what he had thus occupied, it would not only obstruct his natural and innocent design for his own support—which must appear odious, as it is ill-natured—but such a practice becoming common among men would subject them to the greatest misery. What one man now occupies, another without any preferable claim deprives him of; a third person may in like manner deprive him of what he next occupies; he may in like manner be again defeated by a fourth. And thus the whole grant made to him by God and nature of the inferior creatures for his support might be defeated by the ill-nature and injustice of his neighbors, without any necessity; since these neighbors might provide for themselves by their own diligence without interfering with his acquisitions. Thus the first impulses of nature toward supporting ourselves, or those who are dear to us, point out the right of the first occupant to such things as are fit for present use. The obstructing this

Natural reasons for property of a private kind.

Before mankind had increased much, if the regions they possessed were so very fruitful and mild that there was plenty of all conveniences without any difficult labor, there was little occasion for any further rules of property. Nature has given to all men some ingenuity and active powers, and a disposition to exert them; and each man has not only selfish desires toward his own happiness and the means to achieve it, but also some tender, generous affections in the various relations of life. From these strong feelings in our hearts, we discover the right of property that each one has in the fruits of his own labor; that is, we must approve of securing them to him, where no public interest requires the contrary; and we must condemn as cruel, unsociable, and oppressive all depriving of men of the use and free disposal of what they have thus occupied and cultivated, according to any innocent inclination of their hearts.

# C H A P. VII.

## The MEANS of acquiring PROPERTY. *How far it extends, and in what subjects it resides.*

**I. PROPERTY** is either *original* or *derived*. Original property is that which is acquired by first occupation and cultivation; derived property is what is obtained from some previous owner.

<margin>
Occupation and cultivation are the means.
</margin>
The general reasons for property have already been explained, and show the original means of acquiring it: namely, occupation and labor used in cultivation. But to understand the natural grounds of property more fully, we may observe that men are naturally concerned about their own future interests, and those of people dear to them, as well as their present interests. They may be miserable in the midst of present abundance if they have no reasonable assurance regarding the future. The various rules of property as they exist in a state of natural liberty, like all other special laws of nature, not only admit exceptions in cases of great necessity, but may justly be altered and limited under civil government, as the good of the state requires.

<margin>What things are still common.</margin>
V. The origin of property explained above shows the reason why such things as are inexhaustible and serve the purposes of everyone, and require no labor to make them useful, should remain common to all, such as the air, the water of rivers, and the ocean, and even narrow straits, which can provide passage to all ships without being made worse. Where the use is inexhaustible, but some expense is required to secure it, this may be a just reason for obliging all who share in it to contribute in an equitable manner to the necessary expense, such as that of lighthouses, or armed ships to secure the seas from pirates. But ownership of the shores on both sides of such straits can give no right to exclude anyone who is ready to make such an equitable contribution from passing through such straits, or carrying on any innocent commerce with the nations who live within them.

Property in the sea.

It is scarcely conceivable upon what other foundation than a compact, or the consent of neighboring states, anyone can claim any property in the sea, or any right in it superior to that of other nations. Each nation indeed, for its own defense, seems to have a right to prevent any warships of other nations from sailing so near its coast that they could harass any of its subjects in their possessions. But this property can extend no further than a gunshot. Hovering indeed without necessity upon our coasts, though at a greater distance, may give just suspicion of some hostile design, and may be a just reason for protest and demanding security, or for obliging them by force to withdraw to a greater distance.

But is it not folly to confine something to one purpose only when it can answer other purposes and be no less fit for the purpose chiefly intended? The state has a just right to annul superstitious restrictions in any <term>conveyances</term> <note>legal documents transferring property</note>, and to void all such transfers that prove foolish or hurtful to society.

There are just reasons why civil laws should introduce other rules of prescription: partly to encourage subjects to take proper care of their goods and claims in a timely manner while they can still be verified; partly because over a long period of undisturbed possession against some hidden titles, goods may be transferred for valuable payment to fair purchasers, or be subjected to legal settlements, entails, and mortgages for similar reasons, which cannot be overturned without causing great injury to innocent people; and partly to exclude clever and unprovable frauds, which could not be prevented if any deeds claimed to be very old—whose witnesses must be dead—were accepted as valid to overturn a long period of undisturbed possession.

The civil law makes a presumptive title, or *bona fides* <note>good faith</note>, upon which the possessor may probably have believed the goods to be his own, a necessary start to prescription; so that no length of possession that began without a plausible title can grant a right. But the case of a fair purchaser who buys from a long-term possessor without any notice given to the purchaser of another person's hidden title is so favorable, and his plea so fair—especially when he cannot recover his money from the seller—that even if the seller had begun possession without this just presumption, it would be very difficult to dismiss all claims of the fair purchaser, or at least his right to recover the price he paid. Some of the reasons for prescription may hold true even where the possession did not begin with a presumptive title.

The rights to accessions.
</margin>
VIII. Regarding accessions or any additional profits from goods held in property, these rules are obvious. 1. 
> “All fruits, increases, or improvements occurring to the goods in a person’s property, to which neither the goods nor labors of others contributed, belong to the owner, except where another person, by contract or civil law, acquires some right in them.” 

But, 2. 
> “Where the goods or labors of other persons have contributed to any increase or improvement, without fraud or culpable negligence by anyone involved, all those who have contributed by their labors or goods have a joint property in the compound, or in the fruits and improvements, each in proportion to the value of what he contributed.”

If the goods or the fruits can be divided without a loss to the whole, they should be divided in this proportion among those who contributed to them. If the subject cannot be divided without a loss to the whole, it should be used alternately for periods of time proportioned to the values each one contributed, or be used in common continuously if it allows for such use. If the subject allows neither common nor alternate use, it should go to that partner for whom it is of the greatest value or importance, in this manner: first, let the proportion of each person’s right relative to the other partners be determined, and the partner who bids the most for it should have it, after making compensation to the rest for their shares.<note>See cases of this kind in *Cicero de officiis* <gloss>On Duties</gloss>, book 2, chapter 23, and the judgment of *Aratus* upon them.</note>

When, through the fraud or blameworthy negligence of one person, their labor or goods are blended with those of others in such a way that the resulting compound or new form is no longer desirable to the other innocent owner, this owner has a right to full compensation for the value of their goods—now rendered unfit for their use—and for whatever clear profits they could have earned from their goods had they been left alone. If my goods are improved for my use by another person’s goods or labor without my authorization, I am only required to pay for the value of the improvement as it serves my purposes, and not the value it might have for the purposes of the person who wrongfully meddled with my goods. There is no reason that, because of their fault, I should either lose my goods or be forced to pay for more expensive improvements than were suitable for my affairs. The appropriate punishment for this fraudulent or blameworthy meddling with the goods of others is a subject of inquiry entirely separate from the matter of property.

<margin>Real and personal rights.</margin>
I. Adventitious rights are either *real* or *personal*. All adventitious *real rights* arise from a transfer of some of the original rights of *property* from one person to another. And all *personal adventitious rights* are established by transferring to others some parts of our natural liberty, or of our right to act as we please, and by binding ourselves to certain performances on behalf of others. The *real rights* are attached to specific goods. The *personal* rights are not.

The necessity and use of frequent contracts and transfers of property is largely evident from what was said above,<note>Chapters 6 and 7.</note> and will appear even more fully hereafter. The difference between real and personal rights must be explained here, as well as the foundation for this distinction, prior to any civil laws.

<margin>The basis of this distinction.</margin>
One may often be inclined to incur an obligation to another for a certain value, and have every moral certainty and an honest intention of fulfilling it faithfully, while still being unwilling to place any one specific part of his goods more than another in the power of his creditor; he keeps it at his own choice which part of them he will transfer to discharge this obligation. And a creditor may often be satisfied with such commitments from the debtor, if he is assured of his

The creditor no doubt in such a case has a general security from all the debtor's goods, since upon the debtor's default, he may by natural liberty seize any part of them for discharge of the debt, if no other creditor has obtained a real right in them. But the advantage of the personal obligation to the debtor is this: that he is still master of all his goods and still retains the choice, within the specified time, to discharge the claims upon him in the manner he likes best. And the advantage of the real right to the creditor consists in this: that from the goods specifically subjected to his claim, he may be secure, notwithstanding any subsequent debts incurred to others, or even prior personal debts which his debtor may be incapable of discharging.

If one has done any damage to another, he becomes indebted to the person who suffered this damage for its full value. And yet the sufferer has only a personal right, which does not take priority over any claims of a third person, nor does it affect one part of the goods of the one who did the damage more than another. If full compensation is made, he cannot limit the debtor as to which goods this compensation must come from.

<margin>Real rights are preferable to personal ones,</margin>
A just man will undoubtedly observe and fulfill the personal rights of others, as well as the real rights, to the utmost of his power; but the security is not the same in both, as it is abundantly known when different claims occur against a person who does not have the assets to satisfy them. The real rights must take precedence over the personal ones. He who consented to accept a lesser security must not expect to be as safe as one who insisted upon and obtained a greater security, or who would not have contracted or lent upon any other terms.

<margin>For what reasons.</margin>
The preservation of the necessary faith in commerce requires this preference of real rights over personal ones. In the full transfer of property, and even in assigning goods as real securities by pledge or mortgage, there must be such public forms as will secure the purchaser or lender against all prior secret contracts with others, even though these private contracts gave personal rights. No man would buy goods if he could not be secured in the possession of what he purchased against former private contracts of sale. Nor could he be secured if prior secret contracts did not yield to such public ones conducted with the usual forms established for conveying real rights. Nor would men lend upon any pledge or mortgage if there were not some public forms appointed to transfer a real right that is preferable to any prior personal rights established for others by a hidden contract.

Where these confirm a contract, a real right is established, which no personal right should defeat. And yet the person defrauded of his personal right in this way, by means of the subsequent real one transferring the property, has a just claim against the seller who defrauded him—not only for compensation for all the damage * he sustains, but for the † full value of all the profit he could have made had he not been deceived. But without this preference of real rights over personal ones, there could be no commerce.

<margin>Derived real rights are parts of property often separated from the rest.</margin>
II. Derived real rights are either some parts of the right of property transferred to another and separated from the rest, or complete property derived from the original owner.

The parts of property frequently transferred separately from the rest of it belong chiefly to these four classes: 1. *Right of possession*; thus, one may have a right to possess goods he knows belong to others, until the true owner proves his title. This right is valid against all others and often may be turned into complete property. 2. The *right of succession*, which one

As to the right of possession: The possessor by fraud or unjust violence has no right; anyone who intends to recover the goods for the owner may justly dispossess him. But he who possesses without fraud or unjust violence the goods he knows belong to others, has a right valid against all except the proprietor, or such as claim under him. If no such person can be found, or if the proprietor quits his claim, the possessor becomes the proprietor by occupation. The possessor is always obliged to make public notice that he has such goods, and to use all reasonable means to make it known to the proprietor. Designed concealment of them is no better than theft. When the possessor restores them, he may justly demand to be repaid all reasonable expenses made upon the goods, or upon giving public notice about them.

<margin>A confused imagination to be avoided in this matter.</margin>
In these questions, our reason is disturbed by some confused imagination of property as some physical quality or chain between the goods and the proprietor, conceived to establish a more sacred right than many other very equitable claims. And yet it cannot be of a more sacred kind than the rights arising from contracts and fair purchases; since it is by contracts and purchases that property is most frequently acquired: and there is no reason that an innocent man should suffer because of any vice of another in which he had no hand.

Abstracting from such imaginations, property is thus determined by the law of nature; in certain circumstances, we see at once that it would be cruel and inhuman toward an individual to deprive him of the full use of certain goods; as when they were acqui-

In these circumstances, we declare that the man has the right of property. When equal circumstances of specific humanity plead for two persons in opposition to each other, we then consider any circumstance on one side which some remote interest of society may require to be respected; and we judge the right to follow that circumstance. Or at least, when a law or custom is once established on account of this remote utility, we judge the property to belong to that side and do not regard the weaker claim of the other—though a humane man would not disregard it altogether. Other cases happen where the pleas from the remote utilities of society are also equal; and in them, there is no other remedy but dividing the loss among everyone concerned, in some proportion or another.

The contract and price paid—the grand foundations of the titles and pleas of humanity—are the same on both sides. It is equally hard that either of the innocent men should suffer. The lack of obvious reasons for placing the entire loss on one side in this and some other cases will be little regretted by anyone except for such selfish wretches who grasp at every advantage they can obtain without incurring the infamy of direct injustice, and who have no compassion for others.

In general, as far as such possessors are enriched or profited by means of the goods of others, they are obliged to restore them; but they are enriched only by what remains after all expenses they incurred in preserving, improving, or cultivating the goods are deducted. These expenses the proprietor is obliged to repay when he recovers his goods. Goods obtained by donation, succession, or any <term>gratuitous title</term> should clearly be restored without any other compensation from the proprietor other than those expenses for preservation and improvement.

<margin>Right of succession in entails.</margin>

When one who has unlimited property conveys a right of succession to several persons, in a certain series, upon certain contingencies, these persons have a right to this succession just as valid as what people acquire by any donation; as unlimited property includes a right of disposing upon any contingency or condition, as well as absolutely. Such entails may be made imprudently, or contrary to reasons of humanity, and so may donations. Civil laws, however, may justly limit this power of entail as the interest of the state or the necessity of encouraging industry may require.

<margin>
Servitudes.
</margin>
VI. The fourth class of real rights separable from the rest of the property are *servitudes*, when one person has a right to some limited use of the goods of another. All servitudes are real rights applied to specific lands, tenements, or goods. But some are established in favor of a person and only for their benefit; others are established for the advantage of some adjacent farm or tenement, regardless of who the owner may be. The former, based on the subjects of these rights and not the object they apply to, are called *personal servitudes*, which expire with the person; the latter, for the same reason, are called *real servitudes* and may be perpetual. Thus, the use of a house or a farm granted to a friend for their lifetime when the ownership is held by another is a personal servitude, which cannot be transferred by them to someone else. But when a farm is subjected to a road for the convenience of the owners of an adjacent farm, or the owners of one tenement in a town have a right to place beams into the gables of the neighboring house to support the floors or roof, these are real servitudes, which may be established for the convenience of lands or tenements and may be perpetual.† The nature of the contracts or deeds by which such servitudes are established shows the rights and obligations of the parties, which also depend much upon the customs of the places where they are recognized.

---

† See <note>Justinian's Institutes, book 2, titles 3, 4, and 5.</note>

<margin>
*Transfer of complete property in several ways.*
</margin>
VII. Complete property may be transferred either by the *voluntary deed* of the owner, or by the *disposition of the law of nature*, without his consent, for the interest of others. By *deed* of the owner, it may be transferred either *during his life* or *upon his death*. And by the disposition of the law of nature, without his consent, property may be transferred either during the owner’s life or upon his death. We will discuss these four in order.

<margin>
*Voluntary deed during life.*
</margin>
1. By voluntary deed of the owner during his life, either freely by donation or for a certain price or valuable consideration; we treat this in the following chapter on contracts.

<margin>
*By testament.*
</margin>
2. Property is conveyed by the voluntary act of the owner upon his death by last will or testament. This right of bequeathing by will is naturally included in property, which contains a right of disposing of it upon any condition or contingency. Take away this right, and industry would be greatly discouraged once men are reasonably provided with necessities for themselves and their families during life; otherwise, men would be forced into quite a hazardous course of conduct by actually giving away during life whatever they acquire beyond their own probable consumption in their lifetime. Not to mention that they must give it away as soon as they acquire any surplus, since the suddenness of death, or a delirium, may make them incapable of making donations as death approaches. This right, therefore, of bequeathing by will seems clearly founded in the law of nature, though civil laws may li-

The foundation of this right of testaments.
</margin>
That the law of nature and the interest of society establish this right of bequeathing by will is as plain as that they establish other rights of the proprietor. The natural design of mankind in any acquisitions beyond their own consumption is to promote by them the happiness of those they love; one desires that they may obtain this happiness not only during his life, but after his death. These kind affections and suitable services to make others happy, whether we are to live with them or not, are the natural, joyful, and honorable exercises of the human soul while we live. And it is cruel and unjust to hinder a man either from such good services while he lives, or to deprive him of the joyful hope that his surviving friends shall benefit from the fruits of his labors. Concerning succession for those who die without a will.
</margin>
The fourth method of transfer is by the law of nature, without any action by the owner, occurring upon his death in the succession of those who die intestate. The reasons for this are as follows. As is well known to everyone, the intention of the deceased in all his acquisitions beyond his own use was to contribute to the happiness of those who were dear to him. We see that a person’s descendants—and, in their absence, his relatives—are universally dearer to men than others, even though they may happen to have interacted more with others in matters of business or pleasure. When men declare their wills, we see a general inclination to improve the fortunes of their descendants and relatives; we rightly presume the same intention even where it is not explicitly declared. Unless some public interest requires it, it is cruel to defeat this natural hope of inheritance based on blood ties. Our children—and, failing them, our relatives—clearly have a right (provided they have not forfeited it through some undutiful conduct) not only to be supported by us in their state of need, but to have their condition improved by any surplus goods we have beyond our own consumption. It is contrary to nature, as well as humanity, to deny this claim when no public interest demands it. It is also clear that leaving the property of someone who died without a will as common property for anyone to take would cause the greatest confusion.

<header>Derived real Rights.</header>

Book II. must be in some proportion to the degrees of friendship; but these cannot now be determined; and much less could they be determined if the hopes of succession invited all flatterers. We also justly presume the will of the intestate from this: that since the custom has been almost universally established in all nations to admit only kinsmen to succession, had the deceased intended that others should be admitted, he would have expressly declared this unique and less common desire.

<margin>The natural way of succession.</margin>
The natural affections of men show that their posterity should be admitted in the first place—namely, children and grandchildren. Grandchildren, at least, should be admitted to their parent's share among them, where a deceased child has left more than one heir. Along with posterity, parents should be admitted if they are in financial hardship. In the absence of both, brothers and sisters should be admitted, and along with them the children of a deceased brother or sister, receiving at least the share their parent would have received had the parent been alive. Reasons of humanity would sometimes recommend other proportions, but they would cause great controversies. In the absence of such relations, all kindred of equal degrees should generally share equally and exclude those more distantly related.

The customs of many nations and their civil laws regarding these matters are very foolish and have some pernicious effects upon society.
